questions.question: Why is CIMMYT changing its MEAL approach?

options.text: To focus reporting on how many activities were completed.
To show what changed, for whom, and how CIMMYT contributed.
To make the MEAL team responsible for all project results.
To collect more data before deciding what it will be used for.

questions.explanation: MEAL means Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability and Learning. The new approach uses evidence to explain change and improve decisions, as well as report what was delivered.

source.title: A New MEAL Approach for CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Choose one project result and ask what changed for the people involved.

questions.question: A project plans to train seed companies so more farmers can use improved seed. What should its theory of change explain?

options.text: How many training sessions the project plans to hold.
How the training budget will be divided among partners.
Which report will record the number of people trained.
How training could lead to seed use, and what must happen along the way.

questions.explanation: A theory of change explains how activities are expected to lead to change. Here, the team needs to consider whether companies will produce and sell the seed and whether farmers can access and use it.
questions.reviewTip: Map the steps from partner training to farmers using the seed.

questions.question: After training seed companies, which follow-up best shows a change in their practice?

options.text: Check whether the companies now produce and sell the improved seed.
Count how many company staff attended the training.
Confirm that the trainers shared all presentation materials.
Check whether the training was completed within its budget.

questions.explanation: Outcome monitoring follows what partners do after an activity. Seed production and sales show a next step beyond training, but do not by themselves prove improved farmer yields or income.
questions.reviewTip: Identify one partner action to follow up after your next activity.

questions.question: Two projects both measure farmer adoption of a practice. How can they make their results comparable?

options.text: Add their totals because both indicators use the word adoption.
Use the same survey form, even if it does not suit both projects.
Agree what counts as adoption and use compatible measurement methods.
Let each project define adoption and compare the final percentages.

questions.explanation: Shared indicator definitions help teams compare results meaningfully. Methods can fit local conditions, but the team must check that the results measure the same concept before combining them.

source.title: KPI Approach: Comparable and Fit for Purpose

questions.reviewTip: Check how your project defines and measures one shared indicator.

questions.question: A team has limited time to collect evidence. What should it prioritize?

options.text: Collecting the largest possible number of survey responses.
Reliable records that answer its questions and show where the data came from.
Keeping only the summary totals needed for the final report.
Collecting every available variable in case it is useful later.

questions.explanation: The priority is useful, good-quality evidence, not simply more data. Keep records of what happened, where and when, how it was measured, and the conditions that help explain the result.
questions.reviewTip: Identify the evidence needed to answer one project question.

questions.question: Farmer yields improve during a project, and rainfall also improves. What should the team conclude?

options.text: The project caused the full increase because it worked with these farmers.
Rainfall caused the full increase because growing conditions improved.
The increase proves that the project will work equally well everywhere.
More evidence is needed to understand the project contribution alongside rainfall.

questions.explanation: Changes can have several causes, including weather, markets and partner actions. The team should investigate CIMMYT's contribution and explain the limits of the evidence.
questions.reviewTip: List other factors that could affect the result you are measuring.

questions.question: Yields stay the same during a drought in an area supported by a project. How should the team interpret this result?

options.text: The project may have prevented a decline; check what would likely have happened without it.
The project had no benefit because yields did not increase during the drought.
The project was successful because stable yields always show a positive effect.
The result adds no useful information and should be left out of the report.

questions.explanation: No observed increase does not always mean no benefit: the project may have helped prevent a decline. A suitable comparison and evidence about other conditions are needed to assess what would likely have happened without it.
questions.reviewTip: Discuss what a fair comparison would look like for your project.

questions.question: Monitoring shows that few farmers use a practice after training. What should the team do next?

options.text: Repeat the training in the same way to reach more farmers.
Wait for the final report before discussing low use.
Explore the reasons with farmers and partners, agree changes, and follow up.
Record the low use in a dashboard and continue the existing plan.

questions.explanation: Learning means using evidence to improve what the team does. Agree what will change, who will act and when to check whether the change helped; record difficult findings as well as positive ones.
questions.reviewTip: Name one decision your next evidence review should inform.

questions.question: Who does CIMMYT need to account to for its work and results?

options.text: Investors and institutional partners only.
Investors and partners, farmers and communities, science and CGIAR, and internal teams.
Scientific peers and CGIAR only.
Project managers and CIMMYT leadership only.

questions.explanation: Accountability runs in four directions. It includes explaining results and limitations, listening and responding to communities, maintaining scientific standards, and taking responsibility within the organization.
questions.reviewTip: Identify who needs to hear about your results and how they can respond.

questions.question: When should a project plan and budget for monitoring, evidence collection and learning?

options.text: When the investor asks for the first progress report.
After activities are finished and results are available.
When an impact study is commissioned at project closure.
During proposal design, with clear roles and resources agreed early.

questions.explanation: Build MEAL into the proposal, workplan and budget from the start. Project teams, partners and MEAL colleagues need agreed responsibilities so evidence is collected during implementation and used in decisions.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Check whether your workplan names the evidence tasks, owners and resources.

questions.question: On its own, what can a project report confirm, according to section 1?

options.text: That training took place or farmers were reached, not whether practices or yields changed
That yields improved for participants, but not which farmers were trained
That practices changed, provided the figures were aggregated across projects
That benefits persisted, as long as the report was submitted on time

questions.explanation: A report can confirm that training took place or that farmers were reached. It cannot by itself show whether practices changed, yields improved, risks declined or benefits persisted, which is why the new approach works from observation-level records.

source.title: A New MEAL Approach for CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Reread the third paragraph of section 1 and underline what a report cannot show.

questions.question: A regional team spends most of each quarter compiling activity figures for investor templates and has no time to look at what the data say. Which change in section 1.1 addresses this directly?

options.text: From siloed information to integrated data systems
From time-consuming compliance reporting to high-frequency insights for decisions and learning
From work that is hard to link to strategy to credible evidence of contribution
From limited analysis to stronger aggregation and evidence

questions.explanation: The fourth row of the FROM/TO table moves from time-consuming reporting for compliance to high-frequency insights for better decision-making and learning. The other rows describe real changes too, but they target silos, analytical capacity and the link to strategy rather than the reporting burden.

source.title: From Report-Based Monitoring to Observation-Based Evidence

questions.reviewTip: Match each row of the FROM/TO table in 1.1 to a problem you recognise in your own project.

questions.question: Which strategic effect does the framework describe as integrated systems connecting science, MEAL, data, KMIT and management?

options.text: Evidence
Agility and foresight
Impact
Collaboration

questions.explanation: Collaboration is the effect about integrated systems that connect science, MEAL, data, KMIT and management. Evidence is about quality data, agility and foresight about timely insights, and impact about credible evidence of contribution.
questions.reviewTip: Learn the one-line description of each of the four strategic effects in section 1.2.

questions.question: A wheat team in South Asia sees from mid-season sowing-date records that advice is not reaching one district, and changes its extension plan before sowing ends. Which strategic effect is at work?

options.text: Evidence
Impact
Agility and foresight
Collaboration

questions.explanation: Agility and foresight means high-frequency insights informing decisions during implementation, which is exactly a mid-season course correction. Evidence and impact describe the quality of data and the credibility of contribution claims, not the timing of decisions.
questions.reviewTip: When you see a decision taken during implementation on fresh data, think agility and foresight.

questions.question: Why does the framework say MEAL at CIMMYT is different from MEAL in a typical service-delivery organisation?

options.text: CIMMYT reports to more investors than a delivery organisation does
CIMMYT's projects are too small for outcome measurement
CIMMYT's evidence is mostly about training delivered to farmers
Most of CIMMYT's evidence concerns scientific contribution to change in agrifood systems

questions.explanation: Section 1.3 says most of the evidence CIMMYT produces concerns scientific contribution to change in agrifood systems, more than service delivery. Its trial, adoption, genomic, remote-sensing, agronomic and socioeconomic data are the asset MEAL has to connect.

source.title: MEAL in the Context of CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Read the second paragraph of 1.3 and list the six kinds of data it names.

questions.question: A maize breeding team in Kenya holds multi-environment trial results. A socioeconomics team holds an adoption survey. A seed company holds sales records. What does section 1.3 say connecting these makes possible?

options.text: Credible claims of CIMMYT's contribution to yield gains, and learning that improves breeding decisions
A larger farmer-reach total, because sales records can replace the adoption survey
Three separate reports, one per team, submitted to the same investor
Proof that the breeding team alone caused the yield change in every district

questions.explanation: The 1.3 table links breeding results to adoption evidence and lists credible contribution claims, evidence that resonates with investors and peers, and learning that improves breeding decisions as what becomes possible. Sales records add to the picture but do not replace the survey, and nothing in the framework claims sole causation.

source.title: MEAL in the Context of CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Study the three columns of the table in 1.3: assets, what gets connected, what becomes possible.

questions.question: Which evidence function recomputes institutional indicators from the underlying eligible records rather than summing project reports?

options.text: Capture
Quality assurance
Integration
Analysis

questions.explanation: Integration links records across sources, projects, partners, locations and time, and recomputes institutional indicators from eligible records instead of summing project reports. Analysis then applies methods that match the question, but the recomputation rule sits with integration.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Integration row of the table in 2.5 and note its last sentence.

questions.question: A field officer in Mexico removes duplicate entries from a seed-recipient registry and records where each entry came from. Which evidence function is this?

options.text: Capture
Quality assurance
Analysis
Use and visualization

questions.explanation: Quality assurance validates, standardises, de-duplicates and documents provenance and quality. Capture is about identifying the question and collecting the data; the officer here is cleaning and documenting what has already been captured.
questions.reviewTip: De-duplication and provenance are two signature tasks of quality assurance.

questions.question: Section 2.7 says accountability runs in four directions. Which list names them?

options.text: Investors and institutional partners; farmers, communities and stakeholders; the scientific community and CGIAR; internal
Investors and foundations; national governments; the media; the MEAL Review Committee
Investors and auditors; the Data Group; project leads; external evaluators
Farmers and households; seed companies; extension services; regional leadership

questions.explanation: The four directions are investors and institutional partners, farmers and communities, the scientific community and CGIAR, and internal accountability within CIMMYT. Each has different requirements and different ways MEAL supports it.
questions.reviewTip: Memorise the four rows of the accountability table in 2.7.

questions.question: How does the framework want MEAL to be perceived by 2030?

options.text: As a compliance function run by the central team
As an investor-reporting service charged at cost
As a data product owned by the Data Group
As a strategic institutional capability

questions.explanation: The 2030 box in section 6 says MEAL will no longer be perceived as a compliance function but as a strategic institutional capability. Reporting and data systems are part of it, but they are not what it is for.
questions.reviewTip: Read the 'Where will CIMMYT be by 2030?' box at the start of section 6.

questions.question: Two maize projects in Kenya each report a 20% yield gain. Project A cites its annual report. Project B can show plot records from crop cuts, farmer identifiers, dates and locations. Under the new approach, what is the difference?

options.text: None: a report and plot records are equal units of evidence
B's claim is traceable to observation-level records that can be analysed and reused
A is stronger because an aggregated figure is easier to compare
Neither counts until an investor has audited the figures

questions.explanation: The new approach builds a traceable body of evidence from observation-level records, so B's figure can be reconstructed, disaggregated and reused. A's report can confirm that something was delivered, but not what changed on the ground.

source.title: A New MEAL Approach for CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Ask of any headline figure: which records could I trace it back to?

questions.question: A project lead concludes that the new approach means quarterly reports will be abolished. What does section 1 actually say?

options.text: Reports are replaced by dashboards and no longer written
Reports stay as the primary unit of evidence for institutional figures
Reports stay, but only for investors who contractually require them
Reporting summaries stay; the objective is to connect them to observation-level data

questions.explanation: The framework is explicit: reporting summaries stay, and the objective is to connect them to observation-level data that can be analysed, aggregated and used. What changes is the unit of evidence beneath the summary, not the existence of the summary.

source.title: A New MEAL Approach for CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Find the boxed sentence 'Reporting summaries stay' in section 1.

questions.question: A seed systems project in Mexico sets up one registry that breeding, MEAL, the data team and management all draw on, instead of four separate spreadsheets. Which strategic effect does this most directly build?

options.text: Impact
Agility and foresight
Collaboration
Evidence

questions.explanation: Collaboration is the effect defined as integrated systems connecting science, MEAL, data, KMIT and management. The shared registry may later support agility or impact claims, but the effect it builds first is the connected system.
questions.reviewTip: Match the scenario to the wording of the effect, not to the result you hope for later.

questions.question: Which statement about the four strategic effects matches section 1.2?

options.text: They are reached one after another, starting with impact
Each effect reinforces the others
Only impact matters, because that is what investors fund
They replace the four results levels of the results chain

questions.explanation: Section 1.2 says four institutional effects are expected, each reinforcing the others. They are not a sequence, they do not replace the results levels, and investors are interested in evidence and agility as well as impact.
questions.reviewTip: Note the phrase 'each reinforcing the others' in 1.2.

questions.question: A breeding team says its trial data is science, not MEAL, and declines to link it to the adoption survey. What does section 1.3 say?

options.text: Breeding, adoption, agronomic and project outcome data form one evidence base
Correct: scientific data stays outside the MEAL system
Only adoption surveys and project outcome data count as MEAL evidence
Trial data matters for MEAL only when an investor asks for it

questions.explanation: The framework connects breeding data from scientists, adoption evidence from socioeconomics teams, agronomic data from field programs and outcome data from development projects into one evidence base covering CIMMYT's full contribution. Keeping trial data apart breaks the first link in that chain.

source.title: MEAL in the Context of CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Read the third paragraph of 1.3 and name the four sources it connects.

questions.question: What does section 1.3 call a valuable institutional asset that is still underused for cross-portfolio learning and impact demonstration?

options.text: CIMMYT's annual and quarterly project reports
Training attendance registers and reach totals
CIMMYT's scientific data, from trial results to socioeconomic studies
Investor reporting templates and PRMS submissions

questions.explanation: Section 1.3 names multi-environment trial results, adoption surveys, genomic data, remote sensing, agronomic datasets and socioeconomic studies as a valuable institutional asset still underused for cross-portfolio learning. Reports, registers and templates are not what it is pointing at.

source.title: MEAL in the Context of CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: List the data types named in brackets in 1.3 and ask which your project already holds.

questions.question: A team wants to report farmers using improved seed by adding up totals from six partner reports. Which function does this skip, and what does the framework require?

options.text: Capture: run a new survey of all six partners' farmers
Integration: link records with common identifiers and recompute from eligible records
Use and visualization: put the six totals on a dashboard first
None: summing partner reports is the approved method for institutional figures

questions.explanation: Integration links records across partners and locations using common identifiers and recomputes institutional indicators from the underlying eligible records rather than summing project reports. A new survey or a dashboard does not fix a figure built from unlinked totals.
questions.reviewTip: Whenever you see totals being added across sources, check for shared identifiers first.

questions.question: How do the five evidence functions relate to the four results levels?

options.text: Each function belongs to exactly one results level
The functions replace the levels in the new approach
The functions run across all levels, from processes to impact
Only outcomes and impact need the five functions

questions.explanation: Section 2 organises evidence across four levels of the results chain and five operational functions, and 2.5 says the functions run across the results pyramid. Levels say what the evidence is about; functions say how it is handled.
questions.reviewTip: Picture the levels as rows and the functions as columns running through every row.

questions.question: A project submits every investor report on time and considers its accountability complete. What does section 2.7 say is missing?

options.text: Nothing: timely reporting to investors is what accountability means
A higher reach figure to strengthen the next report
A second copy of each report for the regional office
Accountability to farmers and communities, to the scientific community and internally

questions.explanation: Section 2.7 says accountability is more than submitting reports to investors on time; it runs in four directions, each with different requirements. The project has covered one direction and left three untouched.
questions.reviewTip: Check your project against all four rows of the accountability table, not just the first.

questions.question: Which practice supports accountability to farmers and communities, as section 2.7 describes it?

options.text: Disaggregating outcome evidence by gender and age and returning findings to the communities concerned
Publishing datasets and documented methods openly under FAIR principles
Reporting harmonised KPIs to investors on a comparable basis
Making individual and team contributions visible in breeding-portal data

questions.explanation: For farmers and communities, MEAL supports accountability through farmer-centred outcome measurement, disaggregation by gender and vulnerability, and feedback mechanisms that return evidence to the communities it concerns. FAIR publication serves the scientific community, comparable KPIs serve investors and visible contributions serve internal accountability.
questions.reviewTip: For each of the four directions, learn the 'how MEAL supports it' column.

questions.question: A project lead says learning happens at the end-of-project evaluation. What does the 2030 ambition in section 6 say instead?

options.text: Learning is the central MEAL team's job after closure
Learning requires a dedicated annual learning report
Teams adapt during implementation, not only at closure
Learning counts only when an investor requests it

questions.explanation: Section 6 says project teams will adapt during implementation, not only at closure, and 6.2 lists adaptive management using evidence during implementation as well as after closure. Learning is a team practice fed by timely evidence, not a report or a post-closure task.
questions.reviewTip: Read the 2030 box in section 6 and the fifth capability in 6.2.

questions.question: Section 2.7 asks CIMMYT to say openly when its work does not produce real benefits for farmers. What must already be in place for a team to do that credibly?

options.text: Farmer-centred outcome and impact measurement that can show whether benefits occurred
A larger number of farmers reached, so the message is softened
An investor's sign-off on the final narrative report
A separate accountability report that summarises the project reports

questions.explanation: Accountability to farmers depends on outcome and impact measurement that is farmer-centred and disaggregated; without it there is no evidence to be open about. This is why accountability cannot stand alone: it draws on monitoring records and evaluation findings.
questions.reviewTip: Trace each accountability direction back to the evidence it needs.

questions.question: Which source does the new approach treat as the foundation of evidence?

options.text: Aggregated project reports compiled at year end
Observation-level records from farmers, plots, trials, households and institutions
Investor templates and the fields they require
Reach totals compiled from training logs

questions.explanation: The new approach works from the underlying evidence: observation-level records from farmers, plots, trials, households and institutions, combined with geospatial and contextual data when these strengthen the measurement. Reports, templates and reach totals are built on top of such records; they are not the foundation.

source.title: A New MEAL Approach for CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Memorise the five units named in section 1: farmers, plots, trials, households, institutions.

questions.question: A regional lead asks for evidence of CIMMYT's contribution to yield change. The analyst sends a bar chart of farmers reached per district. Which function and rule were missed?

options.text: Capture: more training logs should have been collected
Quality assurance: the logs should have been de-duplicated first
Use and visualization: a map would have been clearer than a bar chart
Analysis: apply a method that matches the claim, and document uncertainty

questions.explanation: Analysis means applying methods that match the question and the claim, such as contribution analysis for a contribution question, and documenting uncertainty and limits. A reach chart answers a different question, so no amount of cleaning or better visuals repairs it.
questions.reviewTip: Before analysing, write the claim in one sentence and check that the method can support it.

questions.question: The framework says the logic of the results chain is cumulative. What does that mean for a proposal's theory of change?

options.text: Each level builds on the one before, and each needs its own evidence
Once outputs are delivered, the outcomes can be assumed to follow
Impact is reported as the total of the outputs delivered
All four levels can be measured from one project report

questions.explanation: Section 2 says the logic is cumulative but that different types of data serve different analytical purposes and do not carry the same evidential weight. Delivered outputs are the foundation for outcome evidence, not a substitute for it.

source.title: The MEAL Framework: From Data to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Read the opening paragraphs of section 2 and note the word cumulative.

questions.question: A maize concept note in Kenya lists "farmers trained at field days" as the project's main outcome. Where does the results chain place training delivered?

options.text: Outcome, because farmers were present and learned something
Output, because training is a service delivered
Impact, because trained farmers keep the knowledge
Process, because field days are an activity in the workplan

questions.explanation: Training delivered is listed among the outputs in section 2.2. The outcome is what trained farmers do differently afterwards, which the concept note still has to state.
questions.reviewTip: Rewrite the outcome as a change in practice among the farmers trained.

questions.question: A seed pilot's chain reads: certified seed distributed, then farmers adopt the variety. Which assumption sits on that link?

options.text: That the seed companies will report their sales on time
That the variety outyields the local check in on-station trials
That the investor accepts the institutional adoption KPI
That farmers who receive the seed plant it and keep planting it

questions.explanation: The link from seed distributed to farmers adopting relies on farmers choosing to plant the seed and continuing to do so. Annex A asks seed systems projects to check that this adoption and diffusion logic holds rather than assume it from distribution records.
questions.reviewTip: For each link, ask what has to be true outside the project's control.

questions.question: What does the system change row of the MEAL Matrix ask MEAL to check for a Small project?

options.text: That the stakeholder and ecosystem map lists every partner organisation
That the coordination budget is proportional to the number of partners
The project's contribution to systemic outcomes and the assumptions in its theory of change
That partners have delivered the outputs listed in the workplan

questions.explanation: Annex A says MEAL helps system change projects build a systems-oriented theory of change and check the project's contribution to systemic outcomes and the assumptions in that theory. Output delivery by partners is tracked, but it is not the check the row describes.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Small column of the system change row in Annex A.

questions.question: For a Small digital advisory pilot, what does the MEAL Matrix say the theory of change should cover?

options.text: Seed multiplication, dissemination and varietal diffusion
Usefulness, behaviour change and relevance
Genetic gain, trial performance and deployment readiness
Stakeholder mapping and ecosystem coordination

questions.explanation: The digital agriculture and AI row asks for a user-centred theory of change covering usefulness, behaviour change and relevance, with usage, engagement and analytics KPIs. The other options belong to seed systems, breeding and system change projects.
questions.reviewTip: Compare the Small column across the project-type rows of Annex A.

questions.question: A Medium seed deployment project in Mexico asks what MEAL will track beyond distribution volumes. What does the Matrix describe for this type and scale?

options.text: Adoption and varietal diffusion at regional scale, through digital registries and dashboards
Platform usage and engagement analytics, through integrated advisory monitoring
Innovation readiness of laboratory outputs, through harmonised research indicators
Genetic gain across mega-environments, through multi-environment trial data

questions.explanation: The seed systems row at Medium scale sets up digital registries and adoption dashboards and tracks adoption and varietal diffusion at regional scale. Usage analytics, innovation readiness and genetic gain are the logics of other project types.
questions.reviewTip: Find the Medium column of the seed systems and deployment row.

questions.question: In Phase 1 of the project lifecycle, what does the project team itself define while the theory of change is being co-developed?

options.text: The selection of institutional KPIs and the investor crosswalk
The classification of M&E complexity in the MEAL Matrix
The configuration of forms and data flows in the data system
Intended results, intervention logic, geography and target populations

questions.explanation: The Phase 1 table gives the project the job of defining intended results, intervention logic, investor requirements, geography, target populations and operational feasibility. KPI selection, Matrix classification and system configuration are led by MEAL or the Data Group.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Read the project column of Phase 1 in the lifecycle table.

questions.question: In the RACI row for developing the theory of change and results framework, which role is responsible for doing the work?

options.text: The project lead
The Project MEAL Focal Point
The Regional MEAL Lead
The MEAL Group Lead

questions.explanation: The RACI row marks the Regional MEAL Lead as responsible and the project lead as accountable. The Focal Point is not yet appointed in Phase 1, and the Group Lead has no role in this row.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Separate R, who does the work, from A, who owns the result, in the RACI row.

questions.question: At concept-note stage a maize team writes its chain as "variety released, so incomes rise". What should the draft add before submission?

options.text: The outcome step, farmers planting the variety, and the assumption that links release to planting
A larger multi-environment trial network to strengthen the yield claim
A counterfactual impact evaluation design with a comparison group
A dashboard mock-up showing the expected income trend by district

questions.explanation: The chain skips the outcome level, where farmers change what they plant, and leaves the link from release to planting unstated. Evaluation designs and dashboards come later in the lifecycle; the chain must be complete first.
questions.reviewTip: Check every draft chain for a missing outcome slab.

questions.question: The proposal is awarded. What happens to the results chain in Phase 2, award and inception?

options.text: It is replaced by the final indicator list
It is archived until the endline evaluation
It is confirmed, with indicator applicability and the minimum data needed
It is rewritten by the Data Group for the data system

questions.explanation: Phase 2 confirms the results chain, indicator applicability, minimum data needed, baseline or panel requirements and evaluation design. The chain stays live; it is not replaced or shelved.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Read the central MEAL column of Phase 2 in the lifecycle table.

questions.question: A draft chain for the Kenya maize project reads: trials run, variety released, 5,000 farmers receive seed, incomes rise. What is wrong with it?

options.text: It should drop the trials step, because processes are not results
It needs a larger reach target before incomes can be expected to rise
It jumps from seed received to incomes, with no outcome level in between
It should claim incomes rise only where CIMMYT is the sole cause

questions.explanation: Seed received is an output and incomes rising is impact, so the chain is missing the outcome: farmers planting the variety and changing their practice. A bigger reach number does not fill that gap.

source.title: The MEAL Framework: From Data to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Trace every draft through all four levels and look for the missing slab.

questions.question: Why does the framework not accept one results level as proof of the next?

options.text: Because once outputs are delivered the next level can be assumed to follow
Because CIMMYT must be shown as the sole cause before a link counts
Because only the impact level needs evidence in a proposal
Because different data serve different purposes and carry different evidential weight

questions.explanation: Section 2 says the logic is cumulative but that different types of data serve different analytical purposes and do not all carry the same evidential weight. Each level therefore needs its own evidence.

source.title: The MEAL Framework: From Data to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Reread the second paragraph of section 2.

questions.question: In the maize chain, one link reads: seed companies sell certified seed, then farmers plant it. Which option states the assumption on that link and a way to test it?

options.text: The variety outyields the check in trials; test by adding more trial sites
Farmers can get and afford the seed and choose to plant it; test with an adoption survey among seed buyers
Seed companies have signed a memorandum; test by counting coordination meetings
The investor accepts the adoption target; test at the annual report

questions.explanation: The link relies on farmers obtaining, affording and choosing the seed, none of which the project controls, and adoption surveys are the outcome-level source section 2.3 names. Trial yields and signed memoranda test other links, not this one.
questions.reviewTip: Pair each assumption with the data source that could show it failing.

questions.question: A seed systems proposal assumes that farmers who buy seed will plant it, but plans no evidence for that link. What does Annex A expect MEAL to do for this project type?

options.text: Accept the assumption, because seed sales are already recorded
Defer the check to the end-of-project evaluation
Replace the assumption with usage and engagement KPIs from the digital row
Define KPIs and check that the adoption and diffusion logic holds

questions.explanation: The seed systems row says MEAL helps define KPIs and reporting structures and checks that the adoption and diffusion logic holds. Sales records show delivery; they do not show planting.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Small column of the seed systems and deployment row.

questions.question: Which draft chain states its assumptions clearly enough to be checked?

options.text: Field days held, then farmers plant (assuming participants can get seed locally), then yields rise (assuming a normal season)
Field days held, then farmers plant, then yields rise; assumptions to be added at the endline review
Field days held, then yields rise, because a drought-tolerant variety needs no adoption step
Field days held, then farmers plant, then incomes rise, with CIMMYT recorded as the sole cause

questions.explanation: Only the first chain names what has to be true at each link, so the project can plan evidence for it. Leaving assumptions to the endline, skipping the adoption step or claiming sole cause each hides a link the framework wants visible.
questions.reviewTip: Write the assumption in brackets after every arrow in your chain.

questions.question: Which pathway logic does the MEAL Matrix describe for digital advisory projects?

options.text: Seed multiplied, then distributed, then adopted and diffused
Advice is useful and users engage, then adoption and behaviour change follow

Where, to whom, with what quality and at what scale it was delivered
A higher total reported more often
Relabelling the count as adoption

Reports both numbers side by side without recording how the two definitions relate
Maps the investor indicator to the institutional KPI and project measure, keeping the institutional definition
Rewrites the institutional definition to match the investor template for this project

They are the only level that investors ask about
They show whether people, organisations and systems are changing as a result of the interventions
They remove the need for impact evidence

options.text: Impact
Processes
Outputs
Outcomes

Outputs
Impact

questions.question: Which statement matches the framework's definition of impact?

options.text: Delivery of products, services and technologies at scale across the project area
Changes in partner behaviour, practice or policy observed during the project
Positive, lasting change in agrifood systems such as productivity, incomes or resilience
Completion of planned activities within budget and on time, confirmed by reports

questions.explanation: Impact is positive, lasting change in agrifood systems. The framework seeks credible evidence of CIMMYT's contribution to that change alongside other factors.

questions.question: Two projects each report 3,000 farmers reached. One can also show location, participant identity, delivery quality and scale. Why does the framework value the second report more?

options.text: It proves that adoption occurred
It provides the foundation needed for outcome-level evidence
It counts as impact evidence
It removes the need for outcome studies

questions.explanation: Output evidence should show where, how, to whom, with what quality and at what scale. That detail is the foundation for outcome-level evidence; it is not outcome evidence itself.

questions.question: A dashboard shows reach rising every quarter while adoption surveys show no change in practice. What should the team conclude?

options.text: Reach growth demonstrates outcome success
The adoption survey must be wrong
The impact target has been met
Delivery is growing but there is no outcome evidence of change yet

questions.explanation: Reach is output evidence; adoption is outcome evidence. The two measure different things, so rising reach with flat adoption means delivery is growing and change has not yet been shown.

questions.question: A national seed regulator revises its variety-release procedure using evidence the project provided. Which level is this, and why?

options.text: Output, because the project produced the evidence

Outcome, because a partner's system or policy changed
Process, because it involved coordination with the regulator

questions.explanation: Policy implementation and stronger service delivery systems are outcome examples in the framework. The evidence the project produced was an output; the regulator's change is the outcome.
questions.reviewTip: Separate the output (evidence provided) from the outcome (procedure revised).

questions.question: A project must report the same adoption result to CGIAR PRMS, an investor and its own dashboard. What should the inception crosswalk show?

options.text: How the institutional KPI, investor indicator and project measure relate, with no silent redefinition
A single label used for all three systems regardless of definition
Three separate data collections, one per reporting system
Only the investor indicator, because it is contractual

questions.explanation: The crosswalk maps applicable institutional KPIs, investor indicators and project-specific measures to one another. Submissions are then generated from the same validated records, so data are collected once.
questions.reviewTip: Read the crosswalk element in 5.4 and the collect-once principle in 4.3.

questions.question: An investor defines an adopter as any farmer who received seed, while the institutional KPI counts farmers who planted it. What does the crosswalk approach allow?

options.text: Quietly adopting the investor definition for the institutional KPI
Recording the mapping and the difference, and reporting each measure under its own definition
Choosing whichever definition yields the larger number
Dropping the institutional KPI from the project

questions.explanation: Projects may specify local scope and report investor measures, but they do not silently redefine the institutional indicator. The crosswalk records the relation and the difference.

Outcomes can be merged into outputs for small projects with limited evidence budgets
Impact can be reported directly from outputs when delivery targets are met
Four levels, with outcomes capturing change in behaviour, systems, practice or policy

It counts sessions instead of participants, and it omits the budget
It reports too rarely, and it uses the wrong unit of observation
It uses an institutional KPI, and it lacks a target

142 indicators in 13 volumes: ten impact pathways and three enabling pathways
13 indicators in 142 reference sheets, grouped under the three Thrusts
100 indicators in 13 volumes, all of them reported under the three Thrusts

Peace
Planetary Health
Institutional enabler

questions.question: A maize project in Kenya measures yield with crop cuts. A wheat project in South Asia uses farmer surveys for the same institutional yield KPI. Is this a harmonisation problem?

options.text: Yes. Harmonisation means the same instrument in every project.
Yes. Only the trial protocol counts as a valid yield method.
No. Any two numbers in tons per hectare can be combined as they are.
No, as long as both share the definition, logic and rules, and document their method.

questions.explanation: Harmonisation does not require every project to measure the same thing in the same way; it requires a shared definition, methodological logic and rules for interpretation and aggregation. Sharing a unit alone is not enough, which is why each record must carry its method and quality rating.

So that every project can pick the method that gives the highest value
Because the Toolbox has not yet agreed on a single method for yield
To let regional offices replace trial data with farmer survey estimates

questions.question: After institutional values have been recomputed, how are results rolled up?

options.text: By project, then by investor
By KPI volume, then by Thrust
By country, then by region
By measurement level, then by project

questions.explanation: Section 3.3 ends its aggregation paragraph with results rolled up by KPI volume and by Thrust, matching the Toolbox structure in 3.1. Projects and investors are reporting audiences, not roll-up levels.

source.title: From Observation-Level Data to Decision-Relevant Insights

questions.reviewTip: Read the last sentence of the second paragraph of section 3.3.

questions.question: An investor asks a maize project to report every farmer who received seed under the institutional adoption KPI, which counts farmers who planted it. What should the project do?

options.text: Adopt the investor's definition for the institutional KPI, since the investor funds the work
Rename the institutional KPI so that the two labels match in both reports
Pick whichever definition produces the higher number and use it for both
Keep the institutional definition and report the investor measure separately

questions.explanation: Projects may specify local scope but do not silently redefine the institutional indicator, so the investor measure is reported under its own definition with the difference recorded in the crosswalk. Matching labels does not make receipt and use the same thing.

source.title: One KPI, Multiple Valid Measurement Levels

questions.reviewTip: Reread the local scope sentence in 3.2 alongside the crosswalk element in 5.4.

questions.question: A project designs its own indicator for digital advisory uptake and labels it an institutional KPI on its dashboard. What does governance rule 1 say?

options.text: It stays project-specific until the Design, Standards & Enablement pillar has reviewed and approved it
Any indicator that uses a unit of observation from the Toolbox is automatically institutional
It becomes institutional once the investor accepts it in the indicator crosswalk
It becomes institutional after the Regional MEAL Lead signs off the measurement plan

questions.explanation: Projects can add project-specific indicators, but these are not reported as institutional KPIs until the Design, Standards & Enablement pillar has reviewed and approved them. A dashboard label, an investor agreement or a plan signature does not make an indicator institutional.
questions.reviewTip: Read the second sentence of rule 1 in section 5.3.

questions.question: A reference sheet requires direct measurement at farm level. A project proposes satellite yield estimates instead, arguing both give tons per hectare. How should a reviewer read the sheet?

options.text: Accept: the unit matches, so the method is valid for the KPI
Decline: the sheet sets valid methods, and satellite data serve calibration or upscaling under documented rules
Accept, but assign the satellite estimates the trial-level quality rating
Decline, because satellite data can never be used for any KPI at any level

questions.explanation: The reference sheet sets what is valid, and the triangulation rule says satellite or secondary data do not replace ground observations where the KPI method requires direct measurement; they are used for calibration, contextualisation, stratification or upscaling under documented rules. A matching unit is not a matching method.

source.title: One KPI, Multiple Valid Measurement Levels

questions.reviewTip: Read the valid methods field in 3.2 together with the triangulation rule at the end of 2.6.

questions.question: Which pair of reference sheet fields tells you how a KPI value is computed and how records are combined?

options.text: Concept and unit of observation
Data sources and disaggregation
Quality assurance and provenance
Calculation and aggregation rules

questions.explanation: The sheet defines calculation and aggregation rules alongside concept, unit, sources, methods, disaggregation, quality assurance and provenance. The other pairs describe what is measured, where it comes from and how it is checked, not how it is computed.

source.title: One KPI, Multiple Valid Measurement Levels

questions.reviewTip: List the nine fields in the last paragraph of 3.2 and group them by purpose.

questions.question: A regional yield estimate for Kenya combines high-rated trial records and medium-rated farm records. How should its quality be reported?

options.text: As variable, documenting coverage and method quality, with each record keeping its rating
As high, because the trial records carry controlled protocols
As medium, taking the lowest rating of any record in the set
Without a rating, since ratings stop mattering after aggregation

questions.explanation: The regional row of the yield table rates quality as variable and requires coverage and method quality to be documented, while each underlying record keeps its own method and rating. An aggregate does not inherit the best or the worst rating in the set.

source.title: One KPI, Multiple Valid Measurement Levels

questions.reviewTip: Read the quality rating column for the region and country row.

questions.question: Why can a sum of reported numbers not answer what CIMMYT contributed to yield change in Kenya?

options.text: Because projects report their yields in different units and currencies
Because the sum is confidential until the annual KPI run is complete
Because contribution needs a counterfactual, modelling, adoption data and geospatial assessment
Because yield can only be measured credibly at trial stations

questions.explanation: The Kenya example in 3.3 lists what the answer needs: contribution or attribution analysis against a credible counterfactual, agronomic, socioeconomic and climate modelling, adoption data and geospatial assessment. None of those is contained in a total.

source.title: From Observation-Level Data to Decision-Relevant Insights

questions.reviewTip: Read the boxed example in section 3.3 and list its four ingredients.

questions.question: Why does the framework insist that institutional values come from observation-level records rather than from project reports?

options.text: Because project reports usually arrive too late for the annual run
Because records keep provenance, so results can be recalculated, audited, disaggregated and reused
Because investors require the raw data attached to every submission
Because narrative reports cannot be stored in the MEAL data system

questions.explanation: The data system keeps the underlying records and their provenance so institutional results can be recalculated, audited and reused as methods improve, and direct observations permit disaggregation and re-analysis. Timing and storage are not the reason.

source.title: From Observation-Level Data to Decision-Relevant Insights

questions.reviewTip: Read the last paragraph of 2.5 and the first row of the evidence stack table in 2.6.

questions.question: A MEAL lead has only three project yield totals for Kenya and is asked what CIMMYT contributed to yield change there. What can she say honestly?

options.text: That CIMMYT raised yields by the sum of the three totals
That the average of the three totals is CIMMYT's contribution
That the highest of the three totals is the safest estimate
That the totals show what was reported, and the contribution question needs its own analysis

questions.explanation: Totals describe what projects reported; contribution needs analysis against a credible counterfactual with modelling, adoption and geospatial data built from observation-level records. Any arithmetic on the three totals dresses up a report count as a contribution claim.

source.title: From Observation-Level Data to Decision-Relevant Insights

questions.reviewTip: Separate the question of what was reported from the question of what changed because of CIMMYT.

questions.question: Which four layers make up the Evidence Stack in section 2.6?

options.text: Direct observations, earth observation and sensors, external and context data, operational records
Process records, output records, outcome records and impact records
Capture forms, quality checks, integration tables and analysis scripts
Project reports, investor templates, regional dashboards and evaluation reports

questions.explanation: Section 2.6 lists four layers: direct observations, earth observation and sensors, external and context data, and operational records. The results levels and the evidence functions are different lists, and reports are not a layer at all.
questions.reviewTip: Read the four rows of the Evidence Stack table in section 2.6.

questions.question: A partner seed company shares its record of which registered farmers received seed packs and when. Which Evidence Stack layer is this?

options.text: Direct observations, because it names individual farmers
External and context data, because it comes from outside CIMMYT
Earth observation and sensors, because the packs are georeferenced
Operational records, because it traces delivery to a recipient

questions.explanation: Distribution systems and partner records are operational records: they give traceability from intervention to output and let you link who received a service to later uptake. Coming from a partner does not make it context data; context data are statistics, prices and climate series used to interpret change.
questions.reviewTip: Ask what the record adds. Traceability of delivery points to operational records.

questions.question: In which evidence function is a record validated, standardised, de-duplicated and its provenance documented?

options.text: Capture
Quality Assurance
Integration
Analysis

questions.explanation: Section 2.5 assigns validation, standardisation, de-duplication and provenance documentation to Quality Assurance. Integration comes next and links the clean record to other sources using identifiers.
questions.reviewTip: Read the five rows of the evidence functions table in section 2.5.

questions.question: Which evidence function links records across sources, projects, partners, locations and time using common identifiers and controlled vocabularies?

options.text: Capture
Quality Assurance
Integration
Use & Visualization

questions.explanation: Integration links records using common identifiers, controlled vocabularies and interoperable structures, and recomputes institutional indicators from eligible records. Capture only collects the observation; it does not connect it to anything yet.
questions.reviewTip: Find the word identifiers in the Integration row of section 2.5.

questions.question: The yield KPI method requires crop cuts. A team has district-wide satellite yield estimates and wants to skip the crop cuts this season. What does the triangulation rule allow?

options.text: Replace the crop cuts, because imagery covers many more plots
Replace the crop cuts if the imagery is from the same season
Report the satellite estimate as the KPI value with a quality flag
Keep the crop cuts and use imagery for calibration or upscaling under documented rules

questions.explanation: Satellite or secondary data do not replace ground observations where the KPI method requires direct measurement. They are used for calibration, contextualisation, stratification or upscaling under documented rules, so the crop cuts stay.
questions.reviewTip: Read the triangulation rule at the end of section 2.6.

questions.question: When does a second source strengthen a claim under the triangulation rule?

options.text: When it measures the same construct, population, geography and period under compatible definitions
When it comes from a government or international agency with a published methodology
When it covers a larger area than the project's own direct observations do
When it is more recent than the project's own observations and easier to obtain

questions.explanation: A source strengthens a claim only when it measures the same construct, population, geography and period under compatible definitions. Being official, larger or more recent does not make it comparable.
questions.reviewTip: Memorise the four matches: construct, population, geography, period.

questions.question: Which required functionality gives farmers, plots, households, organisations, trials and projects unique, stable IDs across projects and years?

options.text: Multi-channel capture
Persistent identifiers
Integration
Quality assurance and provenance

questions.explanation: Persistent identifiers are unique, stable IDs for farmers, plots, households, organisations, trials and projects. They link delivery to later uptake and outcomes and prevent double counting.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Persistent identifiers row in the section 4.1 table.

questions.question: A wheat project's enumerators spend three weeks in hill districts with no connection. Which required functionality covers their situation?

options.text: Dashboards and reporting, with a refresh when they return
Integration, through an import from the partner's system
Multi-channel capture, with offline mobile collection
Privacy, consent and access, with a paper consent form

questions.explanation: Multi-channel capture includes online and offline mobile collection, web forms and low-bandwidth channels, so data are captured in the field and synced later. Section 4.2 adds that the system works offline where connectivity is poor.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Multi-channel capture row of 4.1 and the offline sentence in 4.2.

questions.question: What does collect data once mean in section 4.3?

options.text: Each project collects every indicator a single time, at endline
Each investor receives one consolidated report per year
Each reporting system gets its own form, filled in once
Every submission is generated from the same validated records

questions.explanation: Every submission to PRMS, investors or partners is generated from the same validated records used for institutional KPIs, so projects do not enter the same result again for each system. It says nothing about collecting only once at endline.

source.title: Alignment with Investor Reporting Systems: Collect Data Once

questions.reviewTip: Read the last sentence of the first paragraph of section 4.3.

questions.question: A national partner's reporting system cannot accept an automated link. How does the MEAL data system feed it?

options.text: With an export in the partner's required format, generated from the validated records
With a separate form that the project fills in for the partner each quarter
With a copy of the project's investor report, relabelled for the partner
With direct access for the partner to the raw observation records

questions.explanation: Section 4.3 sets up a direct automated link where the receiving system allows it and an export in the required format where it does not. Either way the submission comes from the same validated records, not a new form.

source.title: Alignment with Investor Reporting Systems: Collect Data Once

questions.reviewTip: Note the two connection options in section 4.3: direct link or export.

questions.question: A wheat project in South Asia tracks sowing dates. Which of these is a direct observation in the Evidence Stack?

options.text: The quarterly project report giving the share of farmers who sowed early
A farmer-level plot record of the sowing date taken during a field visit
A district rainfall series used to explain why sowing dates shifted
The training attendance log for the sowing-date sessions

questions.explanation: Direct observations are plot, farm, household, participant, trial or result-object records, the closest evidence of the actual state. A report summarises such records; it is not the unit of evidence.
questions.reviewTip: Check whether the record describes one plot, farmer or trial, or summarises many.

questions.question: What does the earth observation and sensors layer add to the Evidence Stack?

options.text: The closest evidence of the actual state or change on each plot
A replacement for ground measurement wherever imagery is available
Spatial coverage, frequency and extrapolation between observed locations
Denominators and benchmarks needed to interpret observed change

questions.explanation: Earth observation and sensors add spatial coverage, frequency and extrapolation between observed locations, for example mapping land under practices after calibration. The closest evidence of state comes from direct observations, and denominators come from external and context data.
questions.reviewTip: Compare the What it adds column across the four layers in 2.6.

questions.question: A batch of adoption records arrives without persistent farmer identifiers. Which part of the observation's journey breaks?

options.text: Capture, because the form cannot be built from the KPI reference sheet
Integration, because the records cannot be linked to delivery or earlier years and may be double counted
Nothing, because the project total can still be summed into the quarterly report
Use and visualisation, because dashboards cannot display records without names

questions.explanation: Persistent identifiers are what Integration uses to link records across sources, projects and years and to prevent double counting. Summing the batch into a report hides the problem instead of fixing it.
questions.reviewTip: Trace the record to the Integration step and ask what it needs in order to link.

questions.question: Which sequence lists the five evidence functions in the order the framework gives?

options.text: Capture, Integration, Quality Assurance, Analysis, Use & Visualization
Analysis, Capture, Quality Assurance, Integration, Use & Visualization
Capture, Analysis, Integration, Quality Assurance, Use & Visualization
Capture, Quality Assurance, Integration, Analysis, Use & Visualization

questions.explanation: Section 2.5 lists Capture, Quality Assurance, Integration, Analysis and Use & Visualization as the practical sequence for designing and operating MEAL. Quality Assurance comes before Integration because only clean records should be linked.
questions.reviewTip: Say the five functions in order until the sequence sticks.

questions.question: Why does the MEAL data system keep the underlying records and their provenance instead of only the final figures?

options.text: So institutional results can be recalculated, audited and reused as methods improve
So that project totals can be summed faster at the annual KPI run
So that the scientific and corporate systems can be retired
So that every investor can download the raw data without a request

questions.explanation: Section 2.5 says the system keeps the underlying records and their provenance so institutional results can be recalculated, audited and reused as methods improve. Institutional KPIs are recomputed from eligible records, never summed from project totals.
questions.reviewTip: Read the last paragraph of section 2.5.

questions.question: A breeding team proposes exporting trial results to a spreadsheet each month and re-keying them into MEAL forms. What does section 4 ask for instead?

options.text: Moving the trial data permanently into the MEAL data system
Keeping the spreadsheet but adding a quality flag to each row
Connecting the MEAL data system to the authoritative breeding system
Asking the Data Group to rebuild the breeding database inside MEAL

questions.explanation: Where another system is the authoritative source for an indicator, the MEAL data system connects to it through integration instead of copying data by hand. It does not replace scientific systems, and it does not need manual re-entry.
questions.reviewTip: Identify the authoritative system first, then ask how MEAL connects to it.

questions.question: A project lead asks the MEAL team to build the mobile app, host the servers and write the quality rules. Which part of that request matches the framework's split of responsibility?

options.text: All of it, because MEAL owns the whole data system
The app and the servers, but not the quality rules
None of it, because the Data Group owns everything in the system
Only the quality rules, because MEAL owns the content

questions.explanation: Section 4.2 splits responsibility: the Data Group owns the infrastructure, and the MEAL team owns the content, meaning indicators, the data dictionary and quality rules. Software engineering sits with the technical functions, not inside MEAL.
questions.reviewTip: Repeat the split: Data Group infrastructure, MEAL content.

questions.question: A proposal specifies a web-only form, with enumerators writing on paper in the field and typing the data in when they are back online. What should the team do?

options.text: Build offline capture into the mobile forms, synced when a connection returns
Keep the web form and accept the delay, since capture only needs to happen eventually
Hand the collection to a partner organisation that has better connectivity
Ask the Data Group to buy satellite connectivity for every enumerator

questions.explanation: Section 4.2 requires the system to work offline where connectivity is poor, and 4.1 lists offline mobile collection under multi-channel capture. Paper followed by re-typing delays capture and adds a transcription step that quality assurance then has to catch.
questions.reviewTip: Check every field form against the offline requirement in section 4.2.

questions.question: Two investors and a national partner each send a different adoption template for the same result. What does the collect-once approach ask the team to do?

options.text: Add a section to the field form for each template's extra fields
Run a short extra survey in the national partner's own format
Map each template's fields to the source variables already collected and connect each system
Choose the investor template with the most fields and send it to all three

questions.explanation: For each reporting system the MEAL team maps the required fields to the source variables already collected and sets up a direct link or an export. Every submission then comes from the same validated records, so the forms do not change.

source.title: Alignment with Investor Reporting Systems: Collect Data Once

questions.reviewTip: Read the first paragraph of section 4.3 and count how many times the forms change: zero.

questions.question: Midway through the year an investor changes its reporting template. Who does what?

options.text: The project adds the new fields to its forms and recollects the season's data
The MEAL team updates the mapping centrally and projects keep collecting through the same forms
The Project MEAL Focal Point rewrites the institutional KPI definition to fit the template
The Data Group builds a new collection module dedicated to that investor

questions.explanation: Adjusting to changed requirements means adding or updating a mapping, not creating a new data collection. The MEAL team does this centrally while projects keep the same forms, and the institutional KPI definition is never changed to fit a template.

source.title: Alignment with Investor Reporting Systems: Collect Data Once

questions.reviewTip: Read the second paragraph of section 4.3.

questions.question: A regional dashboard shows an institutional adoption total. What tells you the figure came from the KPI engine rather than from summed project reports?

options.text: It equals the sum of the adopter totals that each project reported this year
It was computed from eligible records with the approved method, with coverage, uncertainty and method version
Each project typed its own adopter total straight into the dashboard
It matches the adoption figure already submitted to PRMS last quarter

questions.explanation: The KPI engine calculates institutional KPIs from eligible records with the approved method and reports coverage, uncertainty and method version. A total that is just the sum of project reports is exactly what the engine replaces.
questions.reviewTip: Look for coverage, uncertainty and method version next to any institutional figure.

questions.question: The adoption KPI method requires farmer-level records. A team wants to report adoption from satellite crop-type maps alone and drop the household interviews. What does the framework say?

options.text: Acceptable, because imagery covers every farm rather than a sample
Acceptable once the maps are validated against last year's survey
Acceptable if the maps are produced by the Data Group's geospatial team
Not acceptable; imagery may calibrate, stratify or upscale but not replace the required records

questions.explanation: Satellite or secondary data do not replace ground observations where the KPI method requires direct measurement. Their valid roles are calibration, contextualisation, stratification and upscaling under documented rules.
questions.reviewTip: When a method says direct measurement, satellite data support it; they do not stand in for it.

questions.question: To support a claim about wheat area under early sowing in three districts in the 2027 season, a team cites a national series on total wheat area from 2022 that uses older district boundaries. Does this strengthen the claim?

options.text: No; it differs in construct, period and geography, so it can only give context
Yes; national statistics are more representative than a project sample
Yes; any official series counts as a second angle on the result
No; external data can never be combined with project observations

questions.explanation: A source strengthens a claim only when it measures the same construct, population, geography and period under compatible definitions. Total wheat area in 2022 under old boundaries fails on three counts, though it may still serve as a denominator or context.
questions.reviewTip: Run the four-match test before calling anything triangulation.

questions.question: Which use of satellite data is consistent with the triangulation rule?

options.text: Replacing the household adoption survey with a crop-type classification
Taking a clear image from an earlier year to stand in for a cloudy 2027 season
Stratifying the ground sample and upscaling calibrated plot estimates under documented rules
Treating a strong greenness signal as proof that the practice was adopted

questions.explanation: The framework uses satellite data for calibration, contextualisation, stratification or upscaling under documented rules, after calibration with ground observations. Replacing required ground measurement or borrowing another period breaks the rule.
questions.reviewTip: Reread the example use in the earth observation row and the triangulation rule.

questions.question: A draft investor report says the CIMMYT variety caused the yield increase in the project area. What does the framework ask you to claim instead?

options.text: That CIMMYT alone caused the change, because the variety was the only new input
That no claim can be made until every other factor has been ruled out
CIMMYT's contribution to the change, alongside rainfall, prices and partners
That the change should be reported as an output of the project

questions.explanation: The framework seeks credible evidence of the role CIMMYT's technologies, partnerships, capacity and services played alongside other factors. It explicitly rejects sole-cause claims, but it does not ask you to stay silent until every other factor is excluded.
questions.reviewTip: Read the last paragraph of section 2.4 and underline the word contribution.

questions.question: Which statement is a contribution claim as the framework defines it?

options.text: Adopting farms out-yielded similar non-adopting farms; the variety, seed partners and advice played a role alongside two good seasons
Yields in the project area rose above the target, so the project has achieved its planned impact in the two seasons
The project delivered seed to four thousand farmers across the area, which demonstrates impact at scale
The yield rise is fully explained by the project, because no other intervention was present in the area

questions.explanation: A contribution claim names the role CIMMYT's technologies, partnerships and services played alongside other factors, backed by a comparison. A target met or a delivery count is not impact evidence, and a sole-cause claim is what the framework rules out.
questions.reviewTip: Check a claim for two things: a comparison, and the words alongside other factors.

questions.question: What is a counterfactual, in plain terms?

options.text: The baseline value measured before the project started
A credible estimate of what would have happened without the intervention
The target the project set for its impact indicator
The national trend for the same indicator over the same years

questions.explanation: A counterfactual is a credible estimate of what would have happened without the intervention, often from a comparison group. A baseline tells you where things started, not where they would have gone on their own.
questions.reviewTip: Say it in one sentence: what would have happened anyway?

questions.question: A project measured yields at baseline and endline on its own farms. Yields rose. Why is this not yet evidence of the intervention's effect?

options.text: Because yields have to be measured on station plots before any farm-level claim can be made
Because endline surveys only count when central MEAL runs them directly
Because baseline measurements are not part of the minimum MEAL package
Because the rise might have happened anyway, and nothing shows what would have occurred without it

questions.explanation: Before-and-after shows change, and rain, prices and other programmes move the before and after too. Without a counterfactual there is no estimate of what the project added, however good the baseline was.
questions.reviewTip: Picture the split-screen farm: which field is missing from a before-and-after design?

questions.question: Which question is a counterfactual impact evaluation designed to answer?

options.text: How much did the project spend per farmer reached?
How far did the practice spread beyond the surveyed plots?
How much did yields differ from what they would have been without the intervention?
What might yields look like under a drier future climate?

questions.explanation: A counterfactual evaluation estimates an effect against what would have happened anyway. Spread across space is a geospatial question and a future climate is a scenario question; cost per farmer is performance analysis.
questions.reviewTip: Match each method family in 2.4 to the kind of question it can carry.

questions.question: A project's outcome method needs a comparison group, but the team says it will sort that out at endline. What does the minimum package require?

options.text: A baseline, comparison group or other valid reference planned at inception, or a documented alternative
A larger endline sample, so that the missing reference does not affect the estimate
Using the project target as the baseline when the outcome study starts
Waiting for the annual KPI run to supply a national reference value

questions.explanation: Element 6 of the minimum package requires a baseline, comparison group or other valid reference where the method needs one, decided at inception, with a documented alternative otherwise. A bigger endline cannot recover a comparison that was never set up.
questions.reviewTip: Read element 6 of the minimum package and note the words at inception in the opening line.

questions.question: A farmer survey and crop cuts both measure yield on the same sampled plots in the same season. Does the second source strengthen the claim?

options.text: No, because two different methods can never be compared with each other
No, because only satellite imagery can confirm a plot-level yield estimate
Yes, because any extra source adds weight regardless of what it measures
Yes, because it measures the same construct, population, geography and period under compatible definitions

questions.explanation: The triangulation rule is met: same yield construct, same plots, same place, same season. A source does not add weight merely by existing; it adds weight when the five conditions hold.
questions.reviewTip: Run the five conditions of the triangulation rule as a checklist.

questions.question: The KPI method for yield requires crop cuts. Which use of satellite imagery does the framework allow?

options.text: Replacing the crop cuts, because imagery covers more area
Reporting imagery-based estimates as direct observations
Calibration, contextualisation, stratification or upscaling under documented rules
Skipping ground calibration once the imagery is high resolution

questions.explanation: Satellite and secondary data do not replace ground observations where the KPI method requires direct measurement. They are used for calibration, contextualisation, stratification or upscaling under documented rules.
questions.reviewTip: Read the second sentence of the triangulation rule in section 2.6.

questions.question: Section 3.3 says every institutional result is reported with four things. Which four?

options.text: Target, deadline, budget and investor contact
Coverage, uncertainty, provenance and method quality
Reach, outputs, outcomes and impact
The sum of project totals and the number of projects

questions.explanation: Institutional values are reported with their coverage, uncertainty, provenance and method quality, and are never an unqualified sum of project totals. The other lists describe planning fields or results levels, not how a result is qualified.

source.title: From Observation-Level Data to Decision-Relevant Insights

questions.reviewTip: Find the sentence in 3.3 that begins The result is reported with.

questions.question: A severe drought hits the project area in year two. The team wants to measure how adopters fared. Which cadence row applies, and who leads?

options.text: The annual KPI run, led by the Data Group
The quarterly evidence review, led by the project lead alone
Continuous data-quality checks, led by the Focal Point
Trigger-based shock-event measurement, led with central MEAL and evaluation specialists

questions.explanation: The midterm, endline or trigger-based row covers shock-event measurement where relevant, and impact evidence sits with central MEAL and science and evaluation specialists. The project supplies source data, context and implementation history; it does not run the impact study alone.
questions.reviewTip: Read the fourth row of the cadence table together with the impact row in 5.2.

questions.question: Maize yields in a Kenyan project area rose over two seasons of good rain and strong prices. The investor asks what CIMMYT achieved. Which claim fits the framework?

options.text: CIMMYT caused the yield rise, because its variety was planted across the area
CIMMYT contributed to the rise alongside rainfall, prices and partners, as far as the evidence shows
The yield rise proves impact, because it exceeded the target set at inception
Nothing can be claimed, because external factors were present in both seasons

questions.explanation: The framework asks for credible evidence of CIMMYT's contribution alongside other factors, which is exactly what rain and prices are. A sole-cause claim overreaches, and a target exceeded is change, not an effect.
questions.reviewTip: When context moved the result, name the context and claim contribution.
