questions.question: How do attribution and contribution differ, as section 2.4 and the glossary use the terms?

options.text: Attribution estimates how much of a change the intervention caused; contribution describes its role alongside other factors
Attribution applies to output-level results; contribution applies only to outcome-level results
Attribution is done by project teams; contribution is done by central MEAL and its specialists
Attribution is the claim CIMMYT seeks; contribution is a weaker claim the framework avoids

questions.explanation: Attribution estimates how much of an observed change an intervention caused, usually against a counterfactual; contribution describes the role played alongside other factors. The framework names both as impact methods, and the claim it seeks is contribution.
questions.reviewTip: Compare the glossary entries for attribution and contribution side by side.

questions.question: A team compares adopters' yields with the yields of similar farms that did not adopt, measured over the same seasons. What does the second group provide?

options.text: An estimate of what would have happened without the intervention
A baseline value for the adopting farms
Proof that the variety was the sole cause of any difference
A national benchmark for the yield indicator

questions.explanation: A comparison group stands in for the missing second field: its result estimates what would have happened anyway, which is the counterfactual. Even a clear gap is the effect of the whole package alongside other factors, not proof of sole cause.
questions.reviewTip: Say what a comparison group is for in one sentence without using the word control.

questions.question: Yields on project farms rose from baseline to endline. Yields on comparison farms rose by about the same amount. What is the most defensible reading?

options.text: The project worked, because yields on project farms rose above their baseline
The comparison farms must have received the intervention as well
The evidence shows no effect of the intervention; something else moved both groups
The baseline on the project farms must have been measured wrongly

questions.explanation: When the comparison group moves the same way, the gap is close to zero and the before-and-after rise is not an effect of the intervention. Rain, prices or another programme is the likelier explanation, and the report should say so with its limits.
questions.reviewTip: Look at the gap between groups, not the rise within one group.

questions.question: A programme wants to know how regional yields might change by 2035 under a drier climate if adoption continues. Which method family does the framework name for this?

options.text: Counterfactual impact evaluation
Descriptive analysis of delivery records
Modelling and scenario analysis
Attribution against a comparison group

questions.explanation: A future under assumed conditions cannot be observed, so it is estimated by modelling and scenario analysis. Counterfactual and attribution methods estimate effects that have already occurred, and descriptive analysis only counts what was delivered.
questions.reviewTip: Ask whether the question is about something that happened or something that might.

questions.question: A 2027 adoption survey of project farmers and a national statistics series on all farmers from 2022 both show adoption rising. A colleague says the two sources triangulate. What is wrong?

options.text: Nothing; two series rising in the same direction confirm the same underlying change
The national series should replace the survey, because it covers far more farmers
They cover different populations and periods, so the second source is context, not triangulation
National statistics should never be used in MEAL analysis of any kind

questions.explanation: A source strengthens a claim only when it measures the same construct, population, geography and period under compatible definitions. External series are valuable for context, denominators and benchmarking, but agreement in direction is not the test.
questions.reviewTip: Before saying triangulated, check population and period first; they fail most often.

questions.question: A team proposes to estimate area under conservation agriculture from satellite imagery alone and skip the ground plots the KPI method requires. What does the framework say?

options.text: Imagery can replace the plots once it covers the whole project region
Keep the required ground observations; use imagery for calibration or upscaling under documented rules
Imagery is acceptable on its own once the Data Group approves the processing
Imagery should not be used anywhere in the evidence for this indicator

questions.explanation: Satellite data do not replace ground observations where the KPI method requires direct measurement. They have a real role, mapping land under practices after calibration with ground observations, which is why banning them is also wrong.
questions.reviewTip: Check the evidence stack's earth-observation row: coverage and extrapolation after calibration.

questions.question: At inception a Large project confirms that its impact method needs a comparison group. When is the right time to design it?

options.text: At endline, once it is clear which farms adopted and which did not
During the annual KPI run in the project's final year
After the investor asks for an impact figure in the final report
Now, in the inception MEAL plan, as part of the evaluation design

questions.explanation: Phase 2 of the lifecycle confirms baseline, endline or panel requirements and the evaluation design, and the minimum package requires the reference before implementation. A comparison group chosen at endline, after adoption is known, cannot stand in for what would have happened anyway.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Find the Phase 2 row in the lifecycle table and the RACI line for baseline, endline and evaluation studies.

questions.question: A project has no feasible comparison group and no baseline for an outcome its method would normally measure against one. What does the minimum package require?

options.text: Drop the outcome from the results framework altogether
Record the target as the baseline and proceed with the study
Reconstruct a baseline from farmer memory at endline
Document a valid alternative reference, agreed at inception

questions.explanation: Element 6 of the minimum package asks for a baseline, comparison group or other valid reference where the method requires it, and otherwise a documented alternative. The target is a wish, not a reference, and an endline reconstruction is improvised rather than agreed.
questions.reviewTip: Read the words otherwise a documented alternative in element 6 and ask what documented means.

questions.question: An impact brief for leadership reports a single headline yield gain with no coverage or uncertainty. Which change does the Analysis function require?

options.text: Remove the number, because impact estimates should not be published
Move the caveats to an internal annex so the brief stays clean
Replace the gain with the number of farmers reached
Add the coverage, uncertainty and limits of the claim

questions.explanation: The Analysis function requires methods that match the question and claim and explicit documentation of uncertainty and limits. Caveats hidden in an annex are not explicit, and a reach count answers a different question.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Analysis row of the five functions table and find the word explicitly.

questions.question: Which report wording keeps the claim within its evidence?

options.text: Adopters in three districts out-yielded comparison farms in two good seasons; the estimate is uncertain and lasting change is not yet shown
The project raised yields across the whole country, as the results from the three study districts clearly demonstrate
Yields rose between baseline and endline on project farms, so the intervention has caused lasting impact in the area
The project met its yield target in both seasons, which confirms impact at scale for the investor report

questions.explanation: The first wording names the comparison, the coverage, the context, the uncertainty and what is not yet shown. The others stretch the coverage, treat before-and-after as effect, or treat a target met as impact.

source.title: From Observation-Level Data to Decision-Relevant Insights

questions.reviewTip: Check every impact sentence for coverage, comparison, uncertainty and the word lasting.

questions.question: Which cadence row covers an impact study prompted by a severe mid-project shock?

options.text: Continuous or monthly data-quality checks
Midterm, endline or trigger-based studies
Quarterly or seasonal evidence review
Annual institutional KPI run

questions.explanation: The fourth cadence row covers outcome or impact studies, contribution and evaluation analysis, and shock-event measurement where relevant. The other rows handle quality flags, implementation decisions and the annual KPI recompute.
questions.reviewTip: Read the purpose column of the cadence table row by row.

questions.question: A flood hits the project area mid-project. The project lead drafts the impact study alone and plans to publish an institutional impact claim. What does the division of responsibility say?

options.text: Central MEAL and evaluation specialists lead; the project provides source data and context
The project lead owns impact evidence, so the plan is in order
The Data Group owns impact evidence once the data system is live
No impact study is possible until the project has closed

questions.explanation: Impact evidence is owned by central MEAL with science and evaluation specialists, and projects provide source data and context. A trigger-based study is possible mid-project, but the institutional claim is not the project lead's to publish alone.

source.title: Division of Responsibility: Project Delivery vs. Institutional MEAL

questions.reviewTip: Read the impact row of the 5.2 table, then the Phase 6 project role in 5.1.

questions.question: In the Phase 6 RACI, who is accountable for contribution analysis and institutional impact claims, and who is responsible for doing the work?

options.text: The project lead is accountable; the Project MEAL Focal Point is responsible
The MEAL Group Lead is accountable; the Evaluation, Learning and Accountability pillar is responsible
The Regional MEAL Lead is accountable; the Data Group is responsible
The Data Group is accountable; the Evidence Systems pillar is responsible

questions.explanation: The RACI line for contribution analysis and institutional impact claims gives R to Pillar C and A to the MEAL Group Lead, with the project lead consulted. The Focal Point is responsible for the project's part of outcome and impact studies, not for the institutional claim.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Find the two Phase 6 lines in the RACI matrix and compare their A columns.

questions.question: Which cadence row produces quality flags, corrected records and a system issue log?

options.text: Quarterly / seasonal
Continuous / monthly
Annual
Midterm / endline / trigger-based

questions.explanation: Continuous or monthly work is automated or routine data-quality checking, with exceptions resolved close to collection, and its outputs are flags, corrected records and an issue log. The quarterly row is a joint evidence review and produces a decision log instead.
questions.reviewTip: Read the four rows of the cadence table in 5.7 and memorise each typical output.

questions.question: A project is in the implementation and adaptive management phase. What is the required gate or deliverable for this phase?

options.text: A quarterly or seasonal evidence review with actions, owners and follow-up
A competency check, a live system and named data and MEAL owners
A validated outcome dataset and an institutional KPI update
An approved MEAL plan and measurement matrix within inception

questions.explanation: Phase 5 of the lifecycle requires a quarterly or seasonal evidence review with actions, owners and follow-up. The competency check belongs to the handover phase, and the validated outcome dataset to phase 6.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Compare the gate column of phases 4, 5 and 6 in the lifecycle table.

questions.question: Which three questions does a decision log entry answer?

options.text: What was measured, which method was used, which quality rating applies
What was delivered, how many were reached, where and when
What changes, who acts, by when
Which KPI, which Thrust, which investor template

questions.explanation: The cadence table defines the decision log as what changes, who acts, by when. The other sets describe measurement plan fields or output reporting, not a decision.
questions.reviewTip: Say the three fields aloud before you close any review.

questions.question: The MEAL data system must hold decision logs, management responses and participant feedback linked to the evidence behind them. Why does MEAL need this functionality?

options.text: It replaces summing project reports
It prevents double counting of farmers
It lets institutional figures be recalculated
It closes the loop from evidence to action

questions.explanation: The learning and feedback functionality exists to close the loop from evidence to action. Replacing summed reports, preventing double counting and recalculation are the reasons for the KPI engine, persistent identifiers and provenance.
questions.reviewTip: Read the last row of the nine functionalities table in 4.1.

questions.question: In the Core Layer, which role keeps the decision and management-response log up to date?

options.text: The MEAL Measurement Specialist
The Portfolio Performance and Visualization Analyst
The Evaluation / Research Analyst
The Evidence Systems, Data Quality and Reporting Analyst

questions.explanation: The Evaluation / Research Analyst in Pillar C supports learning reviews and keeps the decision and management-response log up to date. The Portfolio Performance analyst maintains the evidence-gap register, a different product.
questions.reviewTip: Read the key outputs of the three Pillar C roles.

questions.question: The dashboard shows uptake of 9% in one district against 30% elsewhere. According to the project role in the implementation phase, what comes first?

options.text: Investigate the anomaly, then use the review to decide whether to adapt
Change delivery in the district immediately to close the gap
Hold the figure until annual reporting confirms it
Ask the Data Group to recalculate the dashboard

questions.explanation: The project role in phase 5 is to maintain timely data capture, investigate anomalies, use dashboards and reviews to adapt implementation, and document decisions. Acting on an uninvestigated figure, or waiting for annual data, both skip that sequence.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Read the project role column for phase 5 and note the order of its verbs.

questions.question: Which question goes beyond what a quarterly review can settle and belongs to Pillar C or to a midterm, endline or trigger-based study?

options.text: Are last month's uptake records complete and free of duplicates?
Are intended outcomes occurring, and why do results differ across districts?
Should the enrolment window be extended in two districts next month?
Who is the named data owner for each district?

questions.explanation: Pillar C answers the questions routine monitoring cannot: whether intended outcomes are occurring and why results differ across contexts, through learning reviews and outcome or evaluation studies. Record completeness, an enrolment decision and ownership are handled by monthly checks, the quarterly review and the handover gate.
questions.reviewTip: Read the opening sentence of Pillar C and the last row of the cadence table.

questions.question: What are the three steps MEAL runs for a shortlisted pilot project before it joins the KPI pilot?

options.text: Baseline survey, endline survey and evaluation design
Proposal review, MEAL Matrix classification and base budget
Dashboard build, investor mapping and reporting calendar
Readiness diagnostic, selection check and KPI crosswalk workshop

questions.explanation: Pilots join work already underway, so MEAL runs a readiness diagnostic, a selection check on duration, budget flexibility, system maturity and capacity, and a KPI crosswalk workshop that flags what must change. The MEAL Matrix alone is not enough for a pilot.
questions.reviewTip: Read the entry point text under milestone 6 of the roadmap.

questions.question: How does section 5.6 describe the enabling condition of continuous learning and adaptation?

options.text: Evidence reviewed and acted on; improvements released as new versions of the guidance
Role-based training, communities of practice, office hours and reusable resources
Quality controls, assurance reviews and documented standards across the lifecycle
Defined responsibilities across project teams, MEAL, Data Group and leadership

questions.explanation: Continuous learning and adaptation means evidence is reviewed and acted on, and improvements are released as new versions of the guidance. The other options describe capacity development, quality and accountability, and clear roles and governance.
questions.reviewTip: Match each of the five enabling conditions to its one-line description.

questions.question: Which question should CIMMYT be able to answer by 2030, according to the framework?

options.text: What did we do, how many did we reach, and what did it cost, by project and by year?
What changed, for whom, where, under what conditions, at what scale, and what did CIMMYT contribute?
Which projects met their targets, which investors were satisfied, and which reports were on time?
Which varieties were released, which tools were deployed, and which trainings were delivered?

questions.explanation: The framework says the biggest change is in the question CIMMYT can answer: from mostly what did we do, to what changed, for whom, where, under what conditions, at what scale, and what did CIMMYT contribute. The other options stay at the level of activities and outputs.
questions.reviewTip: Read the boxed text at the end of section 6.2.

questions.question: Who maintains the institutional evidence-gap register, and which body uses it in the annual review?

options.text: The Project MEAL Focal Point; the project steering committee
The Regional MEAL Lead; regional leadership
The Evaluation / Research Analyst; the Data Group
The Portfolio Performance and Visualization Analyst; the MEAL Review Committee

questions.explanation: The Portfolio Performance and Visualization Analyst maintains the institutional evidence-gap register. Once a year the MEAL Review Committee uses the annual KPI run and the register to review the Handbook, Toolbox and Matrix.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Portfolio Performance analyst's key outputs in 5.8 and the third governance rule in 5.3.

questions.question: A seed systems project in Mexico closes its seasonal review with a slide pack of findings and a date for the next meeting. What is missing for this to count as the review the framework requires?

options.text: A revised indicator list for the annual report
An investor-format export of the findings
A decision log stating what changes, who acts and by when
A recalculated KPI with coverage and uncertainty

questions.explanation: The typical output of the quarterly or seasonal review is a decision log: what changes, who acts, by when. A slide pack summarises evidence but records no decision, and a recalculated KPI is annual work.
questions.reviewTip: Before you leave any review, check that each agreed change has an owner and a date.

questions.question: Which cadence row recomputes institutional KPIs from eligible records and reviews coverage, uncertainty and evidence gaps?

options.text: Continuous / monthly
Quarterly / seasonal
Midterm / endline / trigger-based
Annual

questions.explanation: The annual row recomputes institutional KPIs from eligible records and reviews coverage, uncertainty and gaps, producing the portfolio dashboard, evidence-gap register and method notes. The quarterly row is a joint review of implementation, reach and early uptake.
questions.reviewTip: Pair each cadence row with its purpose, then with its output.

questions.question: In the RACI matrix, who is responsible for quarterly or seasonal evidence reviews and adaptation decisions, and who is accountable?

options.text: The Project MEAL Focal Point is responsible; the project lead is accountable
The Regional MEAL Lead is responsible; the MEAL Group Lead is accountable
Pillar C is responsible; the Regional MEAL Lead is accountable
The project lead is responsible; Pillar B is accountable

questions.explanation: The RACI row for quarterly or seasonal reviews gives R to the Focal Point and A to the project lead, with the Regional MEAL Lead and Pillar C consulted. The review is a project-level responsibility, not something central MEAL runs for the project.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Find the phase 5 rows of the RACI matrix and read the PI and FP columns.

questions.question: An outcome study of a digital advisory project recommends switching to voice messages for farmers who cannot read SMS. Which action is a management response as the framework describes it?

options.text: Attach the study to the next annual report so the recommendation is on record
Record what management decided, with an owner and a date, linked to the study, and track it
Hold a learning meeting to discuss the study and schedule another after the season
Wait for the endline evaluation to confirm the finding before responding

questions.explanation: Pillar C ensures evaluation findings are translated into management responses and tracks whether significant recommendations are acted on, and the data system links responses to the evidence behind them. Filing the report or discussing it records no decision.
questions.reviewTip: For every recommendation ask: what did management decide, who owns it, and who checks it was done?

questions.question: Which required functionality of the MEAL data system holds decision logs and management responses linked to the evidence behind them?

options.text: Dashboards and reporting
KPI engine
Learning and feedback
Quality assurance and provenance

questions.explanation: The learning and feedback functionality holds decision logs, management responses and participant feedback linked to their evidence, so the loop from evidence to action closes. Dashboards get evidence to decision-makers but do not record what they decided.
questions.reviewTip: Separate the row that shows evidence from the row that records the response to it.

questions.question: Six months after an evaluation of a maize project in Kenya, nobody can say whether its main recommendations were acted on. Which responsibility in the MEAL team addresses this?

options.text: The Data Group audits the evaluation dataset
The Focal Point resubmits the report to the investor
The Measurement Specialist updates the KPI reference sheet
The Pillar C Lead tracks whether significant recommendations are acted on

questions.explanation: The Lead for Evaluation, Learning and Accountability ensures findings become management responses and tracks whether significant recommendations are acted upon, with the analyst keeping the log. Resubmitting the report or auditing the dataset does not tell you whether anyone acted.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Pillar C Lead's responsibilities on management responses and tracking.

questions.question: Halfway through a wheat advisory project in South Asia, the dashboard shows low early uptake in two districts and the quarterly review is next week. Which sequence matches adaptive management in the framework?

options.text: Investigate the anomaly, decide at the review, and document the decision with an owner and follow-up
Move delivery resources to the two districts now and review the result at annual reporting
Commission an endline evaluation before changing anything in the two districts
Keep delivery unchanged because output targets in the two districts are still being met

questions.explanation: The project role in phase 5 is to investigate anomalies, use dashboards and reviews to adapt implementation, and document decisions, with a review that has actions, owners and follow-up. Acting on the raw number, or deferring to an endline, both bypass that review.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Investigate, review, decide, document: keep the order.

questions.question: At the review the team finds that uptake lags in two districts even where registration was on time. Nobody knows why. What is the right record to make?

options.text: A decision to withdraw the service from both districts, effective immediately
A learning question with an owner, routed to Pillar C to examine why results differ across contexts
A note in the minutes to see whether the gap persists at annual reporting
A request to the Data Group to remove the two districts from the dashboard

questions.explanation: Why results differ across contexts is a question routine monitoring cannot answer, so Pillar C examines it through learning reviews and studies. Withdrawing the service outruns the evidence, and a note in the minutes assigns nobody to find out.
questions.reviewTip: When the evidence raises a why question, log the question with an owner rather than forcing a decision.

questions.question: Monthly checks flag a spike of duplicate uptake records in one district. Should this change delivery?

options.text: Yes, cut delivery in that district until the next quarterly review
Yes, treat the spike as evidence of over-reporting by field officers
No, resolve the exception close to collection so corrected records reach the review
No, ignore it until the annual KPI run deduplicates the records

questions.explanation: Continuous or monthly checks exist so that exceptions are resolved close to collection, producing corrected records; delivery decisions wait for the joint review that reads those records. Leaving duplicates for the annual run lets a data problem sit in the evidence for months.
questions.reviewTip: A data-quality flag is fixed in the data, not in the field plan.

questions.question: A project has trained its staff and partners, but the data system is not yet live and no district has a named data owner. Has it passed the handover gate?

options.text: Yes, training delivered is the deliverable for the handover phase
Yes, provided the Regional MEAL Lead signs the attendance list
No, the gate also needs the approved MEAL plan and measurement matrix
No, the gate is a competency check, a live system and named owners

questions.explanation: The enable and hand over phase ends with a competency check, a live system and named data and MEAL owners. Training is an input to that gate, and the MEAL plan belongs to the inception phase.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Read the required gate for phase 4 and check each of its three parts.

questions.question: A pilot shows that the plot-record form takes too long to complete on a low-bandwidth channel. What should happen next under the rollout roadmap?

options.text: Refine the guidance and tools from the pilot evidence and release the improvement
Let each pilot project shorten the form in its own way and keep collecting
Discuss the problem at a learning meeting and keep the form as it is
Keep the form unchanged until all regions have finished rollout

questions.explanation: The pilot milestone exists to test methods and data collection in real contexts and to refine guidance and tools based on what the pilots show, with improvements released as new versions. Local shortcuts change the method without recording it, and waiting defeats the purpose of piloting.
questions.reviewTip: Read milestone 6 of the roadmap and the continuous learning condition in 5.6 together.

questions.question: Field officers in three projects keep asking the same question about how to count an indicator. Which role logs the recurrent issue and escalates it?

options.text: The Project MEAL Focal Point of the largest project
The MEAL Enablement and Backstopping Officer
The Portfolio Performance and Visualization Analyst
The MEAL Review Committee at its annual meeting

questions.explanation: The Enablement and Backstopping Officer provides first-line support through office hours and clinics, maintains a log of recurrent implementation issues and escalates technical issues as needed. A question repeated across projects is a signal that the guidance needs a new version, not a matter for the annual committee.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Enablement Officer's responsibilities on support logs and escalation.

questions.question: A wheat advisory project in South Asia and a maize advisory project in East Africa show different uptake. Which 2030 capability makes a meaningful comparison possible?

options.text: Reduced reporting burden through integrated data systems
A ranking of projects by their reported totals
Comparability of indicators across projects, regions, years and populations
Separate uptake definitions tailored to each project's investor

questions.explanation: Comparability of indicators across projects, regions, years and populations is one of the eight capabilities, and it is what lets scientists compare sites and synthesise. Ranking totals or using project-specific definitions compares numbers that do not mean the same thing.
questions.reviewTip: Read the eight capabilities and the Science and Impact value in 6.1 together.

questions.question: What is the evidence-gap register for?

options.text: Recording where evidence is missing or weak so the annual review and resource allocation can address it
Listing projects whose investor reports were late in the reporting year
Logging quarterly decisions that were not implemented by their deadline
Tracking duplicate records flagged by the monthly quality checks

questions.explanation: The annual cadence reviews coverage, uncertainty and evidence gaps and produces the register; the MEAL Group Lead allocates resources according to evidence gaps and the Review Committee uses the register in its annual review. Unimplemented decisions belong in the management-response log, and duplicates in the system issue log.
questions.reviewTip: Trace the register from the annual row of 5.7 to the governance rule in 5.3.

questions.question: The framework says accountability is more than submitting reports to investors on time. What else does it cover?

options.text: More frequent reporting to CIMMYT leadership and regional management
Accountability to farmers and communities, to science and CGIAR, and inside CIMMYT
Publishing a success story for each investor at the end of every project
An annual audit of the project's finance and procurement records

questions.explanation: Section 2.7 names four directions: investors and institutional partners, farmers and communities, the scientific community and CGIAR, and internal accountability. More reporting to the same audience adds nothing to the other three.
questions.reviewTip: Read the four rows of the accountability table in section 2.7.

questions.question: A wheat project in South Asia delivers its investor report on time, built on harmonised KPIs with documented methods. Which direction does this satisfy, and what is left open?

options.text: Investors and partners are covered; farmers, science and internal accountability still need their own evidence and responses
All four directions are covered, because the report can be read by anyone who asks for it
Only the scientific direction is covered, because the methods are documented in the report
No direction is covered, because reports to investors are compliance rather than accountability

questions.explanation: Harmonised KPIs and documented methods are how MEAL supports reporting to investors and institutional partners. Farmers need disaggregation and feedback, science needs FAIR data and publication, and internal accountability needs visible team contributions; one report does not supply them.
questions.reviewTip: For any evidence product, ask which of the four rows it serves and which rows remain.

questions.question: In the learning and feedback functionality of section 4.1, what must participant feedback be linked to?

options.text: The investor reporting template and its submission calendar
The persistent identifier of every farmer who submitted it
The evidence behind it, alongside decision logs and management responses
The project's communication plan and its stakeholder list

questions.explanation: The functionality holds decision logs, management responses and participant feedback linked to the evidence behind them, so the loop from evidence to action closes. Identifiers help locate records, but the requirement is the link to evidence and response.
questions.reviewTip: Read the learning and feedback row of the functionality table in section 4.1.

questions.question: Which element of the minimum MEAL package sets the calendar for participant feedback and communication back to stakeholders?

options.text: Quality plan
Data architecture
Results architecture
Learning and accountability cycle

questions.explanation: Element 7, the learning and accountability cycle, is a calendar for evidence reviews, adaptation decisions, participant and partner feedback and communication back to relevant stakeholders. The quality plan and data architecture cover checks and systems, not the feedback calendar.
questions.reviewTip: Read element 7 of the minimum package in section 5.4.

questions.question: An outcome study in Mexico reports 31% adoption across all participants. What does section 2.7 ask you to do before calling that a benefit for the communities served?

options.text: Compare the figure with the target in the investor agreement
Disaggregate it by gender, age and other equity dimensions to see who benefited
Convert it into the number of farmers reached by the project
Hold the claim until the impact evaluation confirms it

questions.explanation: Accountability to farmers and communities includes disaggregating evidence by gender, age and other equity dimensions so that who benefits and who may be excluded becomes visible. A pooled figure, with or without a target, cannot show that.
questions.reviewTip: Read the farmers and communities row in section 2.7 and the disaggregation field in the measurement plan.

questions.question: Which dimensions does section 2.3 name for analysing heterogeneity in outcomes?

options.text: Gender, age and territory
Crop, season and variety
Investor, region and Thrust
Project scale and M&E complexity

questions.explanation: Outcome analysis focuses on contribution, trends, heterogeneity by gender, age and territory, and factors associated with change. The other sets describe crops, reporting structures or the MEAL Matrix, not who changed.
questions.reviewTip: Find the analysis sentence in section 2.3.

questions.question: A negative finding is going into the report. Which addition makes it meet the scientific standards of rigour, reproducibility and transparency?

options.text: A short summary written for a general audience
A commitment to a larger sample in the next study
Documented methods, reproducible analysis and a FAIR dataset
Sign-off from the investor before the finding is released

questions.explanation: Section 2.7 lists FAIR data practices, documented methods and open publication of datasets and findings as how MEAL supports accountability to the scientific community and CGIAR. A bigger future sample does not make the present finding reproducible.
questions.reviewTip: Read the scientific community and CGIAR row in section 2.7.

questions.question: The accountability box in section 2.7 says CIMMYT must be open about three things. Which three?

options.text: Budgets, staffing and timelines
Outputs, outcomes and impact
Reach, quality and scale
What works, what does not, and what it is learning

questions.explanation: Accountability means being open about what works, what does not, and what CIMMYT is learning, within CIMMYT, with investors, with the scientific community and with farmers and communities. The other sets are results levels or output dimensions, not the openness the box requires.
questions.reviewTip: Read the boxed sentence at the end of section 2.7.

questions.question: Which element of the minimum MEAL package records access rules and consent and privacy requirements?

options.text: Data architecture
Quality plan
Learning and accountability cycle
Results architecture

questions.explanation: Element 4, data architecture, covers authoritative systems, persistent identifiers, integration points, access rules, consent and privacy requirements and planned data flows. The quality plan covers validation and provenance, not access.
questions.reviewTip: Read element 4 of the minimum package in section 5.4.

questions.question: How does section 2.7 say MEAL supports internal accountability?

options.text: Monthly performance reviews for every member of staff
Assigning all portfolio results to the project teams that collected the data
Easier access to synthesised information so individual and team contributions are visible
Publishing a ranking of teams on the institutional dashboard

questions.explanation: The internal row says MEAL supports accountability through easier access to synthesised information, for example unpacking breeding-portal data so individual and team contributions are visible. Rankings and staff reviews are not what the framework describes.
questions.reviewTip: Read the internal row of the accountability table.

questions.question: Which pairing matches a direction of accountability with how MEAL supports it in section 2.7?

options.text: Investors and partners: feedback meetings that return evidence to villages
Farmers and communities: FAIR data practices and open publication of datasets
Scientific community and CGIAR: FAIR data, documented methods and open publication
Internal: harmonised KPIs reported in the investor template

questions.explanation: FAIR data practices, documented methods, open publication and evaluation designs that support CGIAR learning sit in the scientific community row. Feedback mechanisms belong to farmers and communities, and harmonised KPIs to investors.
questions.reviewTip: Match each practice in the right-hand column of the table to its row.

questions.question: A seed-systems project in Mexico has met every investor deadline. The project lead says accountability is therefore covered. What does section 2.7 say?

options.text: Correct, because the investor is the party that holds the project to account
Accountability also runs to farmers and communities, to science and CGIAR, and inside CIMMYT
Only the scientific direction remains, because the data have not yet been published
Accountability begins at project closure, so the question is premature

questions.explanation: The framework states that accountability is more than submitting reports to investors on time and runs in four directions. Meeting deadlines covers one direction; the other three need their own evidence and responses.
questions.reviewTip: Reread the opening paragraph of section 2.7.

questions.question: Which practice is listed specifically as support for accountability to investors and institutional partners?

options.text: Returning outcome results to the communities where the study was done
Unpacking breeding-portal data so that team contributions are visible
Evaluation designs that support learning across the CGIAR system
Synthesis across the portfolio into credible institutional evidence products

questions.explanation: The investor row lists harmonised KPIs, documented methodologies, governance over data quality and synthesis across the portfolio into credible institutional evidence products. The other three practices belong to the farmer, internal and scientific rows.
questions.reviewTip: Compare the right-hand column of the four rows in section 2.7.

questions.question: Participants in two municipalities report late seed deliveries. The Focal Point files the reports, and the quarterly report says fourteen feedback items were received. What is missing?

options.text: A link from each report to the evidence, a decision and a management response
A larger number of reports before the issue can be taken seriously
A notification to the investor that complaints have been received
Removal of participant names from the reports before filing

questions.explanation: The learning and feedback functionality requires participant feedback to be linked to the evidence behind it, to decision logs and to management responses. A count of items received shows the channel exists, not that anything changed.
questions.reviewTip: Ask of any feedback channel: what decision did it reach, and who answered?

questions.question: Which design closes the feedback loop with communities in the way the framework describes?

options.text: Feedback collected and stored for analysis at the endline evaluation
Feedback linked to evidence, a decision with an owner, and a response reported back on the cycle calendar
Feedback summarised in a paragraph of the annual investor report
Feedback replaced by a satisfaction score shown on the project dashboard

questions.explanation: Section 4.1 links feedback to evidence, decision logs and management responses, and element 7 of the minimum package sets the calendar for communication back to stakeholders. Storing, summarising or scoring feedback does not return an answer to the people who gave it.
questions.reviewTip: Check element 7 of the minimum package for the calendar requirement.

questions.question: In Phase 6 of the lifecycle, what does the framework ask project teams to do with outcome findings in relation to partners and participants?

options.text: Nothing, since validation of outcome findings is central MEAL's task
Send participants a copy of the investor report once it is approved
Collect a new baseline so that the findings can be checked next season
Support validation of the findings with partners and participants

questions.explanation: The Phase 6 project role includes providing complete records, contextual interpretation and support for validation with partners and participants. Central MEAL leads the integration, but the project brings the findings back to the people the evidence concerns.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Read the project role column for Phase 6 in section 5.1.

questions.question: Pooled results show a yield gain among adopters. Disaggregated results show no gain for women-headed households. Which reading is right?

options.text: The pooled gain is the result and the subgroup figure is sampling noise
The subgroup result replaces the pooled result as the project's outcome
Both are evidence; the breakdown shows who benefited and who may be excluded
Neither can be reported until the sample is large enough to agree

questions.explanation: Disaggregation by gender, age and equity dimensions is how the framework shows who benefits and who may be excluded; it adds to the pooled result rather than replacing or cancelling it. Treating the subgroup as noise hides exactly what accountability to communities requires you to see.
questions.reviewTip: Report the average and the breakdown together, with coverage and limits.

questions.question: Where is disaggregation fixed so that an outcome study can later show who benefited?

options.text: In the measurement plan row for each indicator, before collection starts
In the quality plan, as one of the validation rules
In the handover and capacity element, as a training topic
Nowhere in advance; the analyst decides at the time of analysis

questions.explanation: The measurement plan specifies unit of observation, source, method, frequency, coverage, disaggregation, owner and timing for each indicator, and it is part of the minimum package at inception. Deciding at analysis time means the records may not carry the fields needed.
questions.reviewTip: Read element 3 of the minimum package in section 5.4.

questions.question: Section 6.1 says accountability to participants will improve through three things. Which set?

options.text: Faster reporting, more dashboards and larger samples
Feedback mechanisms, disaggregation and attention to who benefits and who may be excluded
Higher reach, more training events and more partners
Pooled averages, investor templates and press releases

questions.explanation: The partners, investors, farmers and communities row of section 6.1 names feedback mechanisms, disaggregation and attention to who benefits and who may be excluded. Reach and reporting volume say nothing about benefit to participants.
questions.reviewTip: Read the last row of the table in section 6.1.

questions.question: An outcome study finds no benefit for a group the project intended to serve. The investor report is due next week. What does the framework require?

options.text: Report the pooled result now and the subgroup result after the next season
Leave the subgroup out of the report and raise it internally only
Replace the outcome figure with the number of women reached
Report the finding openly, with what the evidence shows and the limits of the method

questions.explanation: Accountability means being open about what works and what does not, with investors as much as with communities, and analysis must document uncertainty and limits. Delaying, omitting or swapping in a reach count all hide the finding.
questions.reviewTip: Read the accountability box in section 2.7 and the analysis row in section 2.5.

questions.question: A scientist argues the negative finding should stay internal because it is not a positive contribution to the knowledge base. What does scientific accountability require?

options.text: Publish the dataset and findings openly with documented methods, since the result adds to the knowledge base
Keep it internal until a positive finding is available to publish alongside it
Share it with the investor only, since the investor funded the study
Delete the subgroup records so the published dataset stays consistent

questions.explanation: The scientific row asks for evidence that adds to the global knowledge base beyond internal reporting, supported by FAIR data, documented methods and open publication. A documented null result for one group is exactly such evidence.
questions.reviewTip: Read the scientific community and CGIAR row in section 2.7.

questions.question: A seed company partner asks the Focal Point for participant names, phone numbers and plot locations for a joint analysis. What must be in place before any record moves?

options.text: A verbal agreement with the partner's director confirming the purpose
Nothing extra, because the partner is named in the project proposal
Consent records covering the use, role-based access and agreed data-sharing rules with the partner
Written approval from the investor for the specific transfer

questions.explanation: The privacy, consent and access functionality requires consent records, role-based access, protection of personal data and data-sharing rules with partners. Being a partner does not replace any of them.
questions.reviewTip: Read the privacy, consent and access row in section 4.1.

questions.question: In the RACI matrix, who is accountable and who is responsible for setting consent, privacy and data-sharing arrangements?

options.text: The Data Group is accountable; the Focal Point is responsible
The Regional MEAL Lead is accountable; the project lead is responsible
The project lead is accountable; the Focal Point is responsible
Pillar B is accountable; the Data Group is responsible

questions.explanation: The Phase 3 row gives A to the project lead and R to the Project MEAL Focal Point, with the Regional MEAL Lead, Pillar B and the Data Group consulted. Owning the infrastructure does not make the Data Group accountable for the project's arrangements.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Find the Phase 3 rows of the RACI matrix in section 5.1.

questions.question: The partner argues that the Data Group should approve the transfer because it owns the infrastructure. What does the framework say?

options.text: The Data Group is accountable for every decision about data
The project lead is accountable; the Data Group is consulted
The Regional MEAL Lead approves, because the MEAL team owns the data
The partner approves, because it will hold the records

questions.explanation: Section 4.2 splits responsibility between the Data Group, which owns the infrastructure, and the MEAL team, which owns the content, while the RACI row for data-sharing arrangements makes the project lead accountable with the Data Group consulted. Neither infrastructure ownership nor a partner's interest moves that accountability.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Read section 4.2 and the Phase 3 RACI rows together.

questions.question: A regional director says each project team is accountable for the region's portfolio-level results. What does section 2.7 say?

options.text: Correct, because project teams generate the evidence the portfolio is built from
Central MEAL is accountable for all results at every level
Nobody is accountable until the annual KPI run has been completed
Leadership is accountable for portfolio-level results; teams for processes and outputs within their remit

questions.explanation: The internal row places accountability for processes and outputs with individuals, leads and teams within their remit, and accountability for portfolio-level results with leadership. Pushing portfolio results down to teams reverses that split.
questions.reviewTip: Read the internal row of the accountability table.

questions.question: A proposal team in Kenya is about to submit. Which set of deliverables does the Phase 1 gate require before submission?

options.text: Approved MEAL plan, measurement matrix and named Focal Point
MEAL section, KPI crosswalk, indicative data architecture and costed MEAL budget
Tested data collection system with approved protocols and consent procedures
Competency check, live system and named data and MEAL owners

questions.explanation: The Opportunity and proposal phase closes with a MEAL section, a KPI crosswalk, an indicative data architecture and a costed MEAL budget before submission. The MEAL plan and measurement matrix belong to the inception gate, one phase later.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Read the right-hand column of the lifecycle table and match each gate to its phase.

questions.question: In the RACI for Phase 5, who is responsible for collecting routine activity and output data and running first-line QA, and who is accountable?

options.text: Regional MEAL Lead responsible; Pillar B accountable
Pillar B responsible; MEAL Group Lead accountable
Project MEAL Focal Point responsible; project lead accountable
Data Group responsible; Regional MEAL Lead accountable

questions.explanation: The RACI row for routine activity and output data gives R to the Focal Point and A to the project lead, with the Regional MEAL Lead informed. Central roles do not run routine project monitoring.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Find the Phase 5 rows of the RACI and note which column holds the A.

questions.question: A seed multiplication pilot in Mexico has a USD 150,000 budget over one year. How does the Matrix classify it by default?

options.text: Complex complexity, Small scale
Standard complexity, Small scale
Intermediate complexity, Medium scale
Complex complexity, Medium scale

questions.explanation: Seed systems and deployment carries Complex as its default complexity, and USD 150,000 over about one year is Small. The modest budget changes the scale, not the complexity.
questions.reviewTip: Read the project type row first, then the scale column.

questions.question: A digital advisory programme in South Asia has a USD 2.5 million budget over three years in two countries. What are its scale and default complexity?

options.text: MEGA scale, Complex complexity
Medium scale, Intermediate complexity
Large scale, Complex complexity
Large scale, Intermediate complexity

questions.explanation: Above USD 800,000 and up to USD 10 million is Large, and digital agriculture and AI defaults to Intermediate. Multi-country work does not make a project MEGA; MEGA starts above USD 10 million.
questions.reviewTip: Check the scale thresholds in the column headers of Annex A.

questions.question: Which commitment triggers the Matrix adjustment rule and moves a project up one complexity level?

options.text: Reporting to the investor every quarter instead of once a year
Reporting farmer- or household-level adoption to the investor
Working in three countries instead of one
Having a total budget above USD 800,000

questions.explanation: The three triggers are committing to report farmer- or household-level adoption, outcomes or impact to investors, running the project's own ground measurement of outcomes, and depending on primary data from several implementing partners. Budget and country count affect scale, not complexity.
questions.reviewTip: Read the adjustment rule in Annex A and list its three triggers.

questions.question: Who confirms a project's Matrix classification at proposal review?

options.text: The MEAL Review Committee
The project lead
The Regional MEAL Lead
The Data Group

questions.explanation: Annex A states that the Regional MEAL Lead confirms the classification at proposal review, and the RACI gives the Regional MEAL Lead the A for that activity. The project lead is responsible for proposing it, not for confirming it.
questions.reviewTip: Read the first RACI row under Phase 1.

questions.question: An upstream discovery project with a USD 400,000 budget over two years stays at its default Standard complexity. What is its base MEAL budget?

options.text: USD 12,000, because 3% of USD 400,000 is above the USD 8,000 floor
USD 8,000, because Standard projects always pay the Small amount
USD 16,000, because Medium projects use the 4% rate
USD 20,000, because Medium projects use the 5% rate

questions.explanation: USD 400,000 over two years is Medium, and the Medium Standard rate is 3%, which gives USD 12,000. That is above the USD 8,000 Small Standard floor, so the percentage stands.
questions.reviewTip: Match the percentage to the complexity level, then compare with the Small amount for that level.

questions.question: A multi-environment breeding project has a USD 500,000 budget over three years at its default Intermediate complexity. What base MEAL budget applies?

options.text: USD 13,000, the Small Intermediate amount
USD 15,000, which is 3% of the budget
USD 25,000, which is 5% of the budget
USD 20,000, which is 4% of the budget

questions.explanation: The Medium Intermediate rate is 4%, and 4% of USD 500,000 is USD 20,000. That is above the USD 13,000 floor, so USD 20,000 applies; the floor only steps in when the percentage falls below it.
questions.reviewTip: Use the Medium row of the base budget table: 3%, 4% or 5% by complexity level.

questions.question: Which phrase states the operating principle behind the division of responsibility?

options.text: Central collection, central analysis, central reporting
Central standards, distributed implementation, institutional integration
Project standards, project implementation, project reporting
Regional standards, regional implementation, regional integration

questions.explanation: Section 5.2 states the principle as central standards, distributed implementation, institutional integration. Projects generate the evidence closest to delivery; central MEAL makes sure it supports comparable outcome and impact analysis.

source.title: Division of Responsibility: Project Delivery vs. Institutional MEAL

questions.reviewTip: Read the first paragraph of section 5.2.

questions.question: How are Regional MEAL Leads placed in the team structure?

options.text: One per project, reporting to the Project MEAL Focal Point
One per pillar, reporting to that pillar's Senior Lead
One per region, reporting to the MEAL Group Lead and drawing on all three pillars
One per country, reporting to the Data Group

questions.explanation: There is one Regional MEAL Lead in each of the three regions: Latin America, Africa and South Asia. They report directly to the MEAL Group Lead and draw on all three pillars instead of sitting under one of them.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Regional Layer paragraph in section 5.8.

questions.question: What happens in early October 2026, before regional training starts on October 12?

options.text: The Senior Leadership Team launches the Handbook and Toolbox in a global webinar
The first institutional KPI run produces the baseline portfolio dashboard
Ongoing projects are confirmed as pilots after a readiness diagnostic
The MEAL Review Committee endorses the first annual changes to the Matrix

questions.explanation: Milestone 3 is the launch webinar in early October 2026, led by the Senior Leadership Team before regional training begins. Pilots start from November 2026 and the first KPI run belongs to the 2027 to 2030 scale phase.
questions.reviewTip: Put the seven milestones on a timeline and check the dates.

questions.question: An applied agronomy proposal in Kenya has a USD 300,000 budget over two years in two counties. How does the Matrix classify it by default?

options.text: Intermediate complexity, Medium scale, because the budget is modest
Complex complexity, Small scale, because it runs in one country
Complex complexity, Medium scale
Standard complexity, Medium scale, because it is a two-year pilot

questions.explanation: Applied agronomy and farming systems defaults to Complex, and USD 300,000 over two years falls in the Medium band of about USD 280,000 to 800,000 and 1.5 to 3 years. Budget and duration set the scale; the project type sets the complexity.
questions.reviewTip: Classify in two steps: type gives complexity, then budget and duration give scale.

questions.question: A breeding acceleration programme has a USD 900,000 budget over four years in three countries. What does the Matrix return?

options.text: Large scale, Intermediate complexity by default
MEGA scale, because it is multi-country and multi-year
Large scale, Complex complexity, because Large projects are always Complex
Medium scale, Intermediate complexity, because it runs under USD 1 million

questions.explanation: Above USD 800,000 and up to USD 10 million is Large, and breeding and varietal development defaults to Intermediate. Scale does not raise complexity; only the adjustment rule's three triggers do.
questions.reviewTip: Keep the two axes separate: scale from the column headers, complexity from the row.

questions.question: A Medium digital advisory project at Intermediate complexity will depend on primary data from four implementing partners. What does the adjustment rule require?

options.text: It stays Intermediate, because the project type fixes the level
It moves up one level to Complex, and stays Medium
It moves up to Large scale, because more partners mean more reach
It moves only if the project lead agrees to the higher budget

questions.explanation: Depending on primary data from several implementing partners is one of the three triggers, so the project moves up one complexity level to Complex. Scale is unchanged, and the Regional MEAL Lead confirms the classification rather than the project lead choosing it.
questions.reviewTip: Check the three triggers; partner data dependence is the third.

questions.question: A wheat project in South Asia wants to estimate yield from farmer recall instead of the crop cuts the KPI reference sheet requires. Who is accountable for granting that exception?

options.text: The project lead, because the project owns its output evidence
The Regional MEAL Lead, because the region reviews proposals
The Data Group, because it owns the data system
The MEAL Group Lead, with Pillar A responsible for the work

questions.explanation: Governance rule 3 makes the MEAL Group Lead accountable for exceptions to KPI methods, and the RACI row for KPI method exceptions gives R to Pillar A and A to the Group Lead. The project lead and Regional MEAL Lead are consulted, not deciding.
questions.reviewTip: Read governance rule 3 and the KPI method exceptions row of the RACI.

questions.question: A regional seed deployment project has a USD 500,000 budget over three years and confirmed Complex complexity. What is its base MEAL budget?

options.text: USD 18,000, the Complex minimum, because Medium Complex projects always pay the floor
USD 15,000, which is 3% of the budget
USD 25,000, which is 5% of the budget and above the floor
USD 20,000, which is 4% of the budget

questions.explanation: The Medium Complex rate is 5%, and 5% of USD 500,000 is USD 25,000, which is above the USD 18,000 Small Complex amount. The floor only replaces the percentage when the percentage is lower.
questions.reviewTip: Compute the percentage, then take the larger of that and the Small amount.

questions.question: A breeding project has a USD 290,000 budget over 18 months at Intermediate complexity. What base MEAL budget applies?

options.text: USD 11,600, which is 4% of the budget
USD 8,700, which is 3% of the budget
USD 13,000, because 4% falls below the Small Intermediate amount
USD 18,000, because any Medium project pays the highest floor

questions.explanation: USD 290,000 over 18 months is Medium, and 4% of it is USD 11,600, which is below the USD 13,000 Small Intermediate amount, so the floor applies. The floor is the Small amount for the same complexity level, not the highest Small amount.
questions.reviewTip: The phrase to remember is: never less than the Small amount for the same complexity level.

questions.question: A multi-country applied agronomy programme has a USD 3 million budget over four years. How is its MEAL budget set?

options.text: Co-designed with the MEAL team from the start of proposal development
At 5% of the total budget, which is USD 150,000
At the fixed USD 18,000 Complex amount for the project lifetime
Agreed with the MEAL team after the award, during inception

questions.explanation: Above USD 800,000 and up to USD 10 million is Large, and the table says Large budgets are co-designed with MEAL from the start of proposal development. There is no percentage or fixed amount for Large projects in section 5.10.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Large row of the base budget table.

questions.question: A MEGA proposal of USD 12 million over five years budgets USD 27,000 in total for institutional MEAL. What is wrong?

options.text: Nothing, USD 27,000 is the fixed MEGA amount
It should be 5% of the budget instead
It should be USD 18,000, the highest fixed amount
The USD 27,000 is a minimum per project year, on top of project-specific MEAL work

questions.explanation: MEGA budgets are co-designed and cover project-specific MEAL work plus an institutional contribution, charged as Core Layer staff time, of at least USD 27,000 per project year. Over five years that contribution alone is at least USD 135,000.
questions.reviewTip: Read the MEGA row and note the words per project year.

questions.question: A project lead in Kenya asks the central MEAL team to run the project's routine output monitoring, arguing the base contribution already pays for it. What does the framework say?

options.text: Yes, routine monitoring is an institutional service covered by the base contribution
No, routine monitoring stays with the project; the team can run it as an extended service charged at cost
Yes, once the project is classified as Complex the centre takes over data collection
No, routine monitoring is the Regional MEAL Lead's job

questions.explanation: The base contribution pays for standards, proposal review, quality assurance, integration and portfolio and investor reporting, and project teams remain responsible for routine monitoring. Running project monitoring is listed among the extended services charged at cost.
questions.reviewTip: Compare what the base contribution buys with the extended services list in 5.10.

questions.question: A project wants to redefine the institutional yield KPI so that it matches the investor's template. What does governance rule 1 require?

options.text: The project may redefine it locally as long as the investor agrees
The Regional MEAL Lead can approve the new definition for the region
No KPI is redefined without MEAL team review; approved changes appear in a new Handbook version
The Data Group updates the KPI engine to the investor definition

questions.explanation: Rule 1 says no institutional KPI is added or redefined without review by the MEAL team, and approved changes are published in a new version of the Handbook. The project can report the investor measure through the crosswalk without touching the institutional definition.
questions.reviewTip: Read governance rule 1 and the crosswalk element of the minimum package.

questions.question: How are Project MEAL Focal Points positioned in the structure?

options.text: Embedded in and funded by major projects, applying institutional standards with guidance from the Regional MEAL Lead
Counted among the thirteen Core and Regional positions and funded centrally
Hired by the Core Layer to run project monitoring from headquarters
Placed under Pillar B to maintain the institutional data dictionary

questions.explanation: Focal Points form the Extended MEAL Network; they are embedded in and funded by major projects and receive technical guidance from their Regional MEAL Lead. The thirteen positions are the Core and Regional Layers only.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Project Layer paragraph in section 5.8.

questions.question: A project leaves inception with a results chain, a crosswalk and a measurement plan, and plans to add the baseline and the learning calendar at the endline. Is that acceptable?

options.text: Yes, the baseline can be reconstructed from recall at the endline
No, all eight package elements are in place at inception; none is left to end-of-project reporting
Yes, Small projects only need the first three elements
No, but only the baseline is mandatory; the learning calendar is optional

questions.explanation: Section 5.4 lists eight elements every project leaves inception with, including a baseline or documented alternative and a learning and accountability cycle. Depth varies by scale, but none of the elements is left to end-of-project reporting.
questions.reviewTip: Count the eight elements and check each against your inception plan.

questions.question: Which list names the five enabling conditions in section 5.6?

options.text: Investor compliance, annual reporting, central monitoring, audits, dashboards
Strong data systems, clear roles and governance, quality and accountability, capacity development, continuous learning and adaptation
Bridge funding, new hires, software licences, consultants, regional offices
Theory of change, crosswalk, measurement plan, baseline, handover

questions.explanation: The five conditions are strong data systems, clear roles and governance, quality and accountability, capacity development, and continuous learning and adaptation. Option d lists elements of the minimum package, not enabling conditions.
questions.reviewTip: Read the five boxes in section 5.6.

questions.question: A concept note is due in December 2026. What is the entry point for new proposals on the roadmap?

options.text: MEAL joins at inception, after the award, to build the plan
A readiness diagnostic and a selection check on remaining duration
The investor's template sets the indicators; MEAL maps them later
The proposal goes through the MEAL team at concept-note stage using the Matrix

questions.explanation: From October 2026 every proposal goes through the MEAL team at concept-note stage using the MEAL Matrix, which returns support, KPIs, deliverables and base budget. The readiness diagnostic and selection check are the entry point for ongoing projects joining as pilots.
questions.reviewTip: Compare the entry points under milestones 5 and 6.

questions.question: On the operating cadence, what does a quarterly or seasonal evidence review produce?

options.text: A portfolio dashboard and the evidence-gap register
Quality flags and a system issue log
A decision log: what changes, who acts, by when
Evaluation findings and an updated impact narrative

questions.explanation: The quarterly or seasonal review is a joint look at implementation, reach, early uptake and emerging outcomes, and its output is a decision log. Quality flags come from monthly checks, the dashboard and gap register from the annual run, and evaluation findings from trigger-based studies.
questions.reviewTip: Match each cadence row to its typical output in the 5.7 table.
